lean.statement: (i) On the unit sphere $S^n \subseteq \mathbb R^{n+1}$, $n \ge 1$, with the induced metric: for unit vectors $p \perp u$ and $L \in \mathbb R$, the great circle $c(t) = \cos(Lt)\,p + \sin(Lt)\,u$ is a geodesic on $\mathbb R$; and for any $p, q$, every geodesic $\gamma \in \Omega(S^n; p, q)$ agrees on $[0, 1]$ with such a great circle, with $L \ge 0$. For $q \ne \pm p$ the geodesics from $p$ to $q$ are, up to their values off $[0, 1]$, the arcs $\gamma_0, \gamma_1, \dots$ of V10.23, with strictly increasing energies: infinitely many geodesics. (ii) If every tangent space of $N \subseteq V$ is $V$ (an open subset of $V$, with the flat metric) and the segment from $p$ to $q$ lies in $N$, then $t \mapsto p + t(q - p)$ is a geodesic of $\Omega(N; p, q)$ and every geodesic of $\Omega(N; p, q)$ agrees with it on $[0, 1]$: the geodesics of $V$ are the straight lines.

diff: The verified Chapter 7 lists the examples as not formalized; the sphere and flat open sets are treated in Chapter 10, for the index computation of Corollary 17.4 (V10.23) and the counterexample to Corollary 17.5 (V10.27).

Not formalized: the continuum of minimal geodesics between antipodal points; the minimality of the short arc $\gamma_0$, which follows from V7.30 and the list of geodesics but is not stated; meridians of surfaces of revolution; the cylinder.
The great circles are found from the uniqueness of geodesics with given initial data (V7.5, V9.9), not by Milnor's reflection argument.

items.title: The path space and its “tangent spaces”

milnor.label: §11, p. 67
milnor.statement: $\Omega(M; p, q)$ is the set of piecewise smooth paths $\omega : [0, 1] \to M$ from $p$ to $q$, each $\omega|[t_{i-1}, t_i]$ of class $C^\infty$ for some subdivision. Milnor thinks of $\Omega$ as "something like an infinite dimensional manifold", to be topologized only in §16, and defines its "tangent space" $T\Omega_\omega$ as the vector space of piecewise smooth vector fields $W$ along $\omega$ with $W(0) = 0$ and $W(1) = 0$.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric ($P_x$ the projection onto $T_xN$, extended by $P_x = 0$ off $N$): for $p, q \in V$, $\Omega(N; p, q)$ is the set of maps $\omega : \mathbb R \to V$ that are piecewise smooth on $[0, 1]$ (V7.11), with $\omega(t) \in N$ for $t \in [0, 1]$, $\omega(0) = p$ and $\omega(1) = q$. For a map $\omega$, $T\Omega_\omega$ is the real vector space of maps $W$ that are piecewise smooth on $[0, 1]$ and tangent along $\omega$ ($P_{\omega(t)}W(t) = W(t)$ for $t \in [0, 1]$), with $W(0) = W(1) = 0$; it depends only on $\omega$ on $[0, 1]$.

chips: $\Omega$ has no manifold structure, here too
diff: As in the book, $\Omega$ carries no topology or manifold structure here; $T\Omega_\omega$ is *defined* as a space of fields and is related to $\Omega$ only through variations (V8.2–V8.3).
Paths and fields are maps on $\mathbb R$ considered on $[0, 1]$, and the subdivision is a finite set of break points; the break points of a field need not be those of $\omega$.
Smoothness on a closed piece means one-sided derivatives at its ends, which the book leaves implicit.

items.title: Variations and variation fields

milnor.label: §11, p. 68
milnor.statement: A variation of $\omega$ keeping the end points fixed is a map $\bar\alpha : (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \to \Omega$ with $\bar\alpha(0) = \omega$ and a subdivision $0 = t_0 < \dots < t_k = 1$ such that $\alpha(u, t) = \bar\alpha(u)(t)$ is $C^\infty$ on each strip $(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \times [t_{i-1}, t_i]$; an $n$-parameter variation replaces $(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon)$ by a neighbourhood of $0$ in $\mathbb R^n$. The variation vector field is $W_t = \frac{\partial\alpha}{\partial u}(0, t)$, and "clearly" $W \in T\Omega_\omega$.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $P$ be a real normed space (Milnor's $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb R^n$) and $U \ni 0$ open in $P$. A map $\alpha(u, t)$ is a variation with break points $B$ (a finite set) if $\alpha(u, t) \in N$ for $u \in U$, $t \in [0, 1]$; $\alpha(u, 0)$ and $\alpha(u, 1)$ do not depend on $u \in U$; and $\alpha$ is $C^\infty$ on every closed strip $U \times [s, t]$, $0 \le s < t \le 1$, with no point of $B$ in $(s, t)$. Every $\alpha(u, \cdot)$ then lies in $\Omega(N; \omega(0), \omega(1))$, $\omega = \alpha(0, \cdot)$, and composing with a smooth map into $P$ sending $0$ into $U$ gives a variation again. For $P = \mathbb R$, $W_t = \frac{\partial\alpha}{\partial u}(0, t)$ lies in $T\Omega_\omega$, and every $\frac{\partial\alpha}{\partial u}(u, t)$ is tangent to $N$ at $\alpha(u, t)$.

chips: any open parameter set, any normed space
diff: The parameter set is any open set containing $0$ in any real normed space, which covers Milnor's $1$- and $n$-parameter variations at once.

Behind "clearly": $W$ is continuous at a break point because both adjacent strips compute the velocity of the same curve $u \mapsto \alpha(u, t_i)$, tangent because that curve lies in $N$, and zero at the ends because they are fixed.

items.title: Lemma 11.A: every family of tangent fields comes from one variation

milnor.label: §11, pp. 68 and 74
milnor.statement: Given $W \in T\Omega_\omega$ there is a variation with $\bar\alpha(0) = \omega$ and $\frac{d\bar\alpha}{du}(0) = W$: "in fact one can set" $\bar\alpha(u)(t) = \exp_{\omega(t)}(uW_t)$ (p. 68). On p. 74, 2-parameter variations with prescribed variation fields $W_1$, $W_2$ are chosen without comment.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $\omega \in \Omega(N; p, q)$, $P$ a real normed space, and $\Lambda$ a family, piecewise smooth on $[0, 1]$, of continuous linear maps $\Lambda(t) : P \to V$ with values in $T_{\omega(t)}N$ and $\Lambda(0) = \Lambda(1) = 0$. There are $\varepsilon > 0$ and a finite set $B$ such that $\alpha(u, t) = \exp_{\omega(t)}(\Lambda(t)u)$ is a variation with break points $B$ on the ball $\|u\| < \varepsilon$, with $\alpha(0, t) = \omega(t)$ and derivative $\Lambda(t)$ in $u$ at $u = 0$, for $t \in [0, 1]$. In particular every $W \in T\Omega_\omega$ is the variation field of $\exp_{\omega(t)}(uW_t)$, $|u| < \varepsilon$, and any $W_1, W_2 \in T\Omega_\omega$ are the variation fields of the 2-parameter variation $\exp_{\omega(t)}(u_1W_1(t) + u_2W_2(t))$.

diff: Any number of parameters (the exposition's Lemma 11.A); Milnor states the one-parameter case and uses the two-parameter case.

$\exp$ is defined only near the zero section (V7.8), so $\varepsilon$ must be chosen uniformly along $\omega$, by the compactness of $\omega([0, 1])$ and a bound for $\|\Lambda\|$; completeness of $N$ is not needed.
The derivative in $u$ at $0$ is $\Lambda(t)$ because $d(\exp_q)_0$ is the inclusion of $T_qN$ (V7.8).

items.title: Critical paths of the energy

milnor.label: §11, p. 69
milnor.statement: A path $\omega$ is a critical path of a function $F : \Omega \to \mathbb R$ if and only if $\frac{dF(\bar\alpha(u))}{du}\big|_{u=0}$ is zero for every variation $\bar\alpha$ of $\omega$.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: a map $\omega$ is a critical path of the energy $E$ (V8.5) if for every 1-parameter variation $\alpha$ with $\alpha(0, t) = \omega(t)$ for $t \in [0, 1]$, the function $u \mapsto E(\alpha(u, \cdot))$ is differentiable at $0$ with derivative $0$.

diff: Critical paths are defined for the energy only, the case of Corollary 12.3; Milnor's definition is for any function on $\Omega$.
The definition asks that the derivative exist; for $E$ it always does (V8.9).

items.title: Energy and length

milnor.label: §12, p. 70
milnor.statement: For $\omega \in \Omega$ and $0 \le a < b \le 1$, the energy from $a$ to $b$ is $E_a^b(\omega) = \int_a^b\|d\omega/dt\|^2\,dt$, $E = E_0^1$, and $L_a^b$ is the arc length. By Schwarz's inequality $(L_a^b)^2 \le (b - a)E_a^b$, with equality if and only if $\|d\omega/dt\|$ is constant, that is, if and only if the parameter $t$ is proportional to arc length.

lean.statement: For a map $c$ into a real normed space and $a \le b$, $E_a^b(c) = \int_a^b\|c'(t)\|^2\,dt$, $E = E_0^1$, and $L_a^b(c)$ is the length of V7.11. If $c$ is piecewise smooth on $[a, b]$, then $(L_a^b(c))^2 \le (b - a)E_a^b(c)$, with equality iff $\|c'\|$ takes one and the same value at every point of $(a, b)$ where $c$ is differentiable. An admissible path of constant speed $k$ there has $E_a^b = k^2(b - a)$.

diff: Any $a \le b$ and any normed target, where Milnor has $0 \le a < b \le 1$ and paths in $M$.

For a speed that is only piecewise continuous, "constant" can only mean constant off the break points; the formal equality condition says so. The proof is the variance identity $(b - a)\int_a^b(g - \bar g)^2 = (b - a)E_a^b - (L_a^b)^2$, $g = \|c'\|$ (the exposition's Lemma 12.A).

items.title: Lemma 12.1: the energy at a minimal geodesic

milnor.label: §12, Lemma 12.1
milnor.statement: Let $M$ be complete and $p, q \in M$ at distance $d$. Then the energy function $E : \Omega(M; p, q) \to \mathbb R$ takes on its minimum $d^2$ precisely on the set of minimal geodesics from $p$ to $q$. The proof is the chain $E(\gamma) = L(\gamma)^2 \le L(\omega)^2 \le E(\omega)$ for a minimal geodesic $\gamma$, with the equality cases.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: a path $\gamma \in \Omega(N; p, q)$ is *minimal* if $L(\gamma) \le L(\omega)$ for every $\omega \in \Omega(N; p, q)$. If $\gamma$ is minimal and a geodesic of $\Omega$ (V8.10), then $E(\gamma) \le E(\omega)$ for every $\omega \in \Omega(N; p, q)$.

diff: Only the inequality is formalized. Neither the value $d^2$ of the minimum nor the converse (a path of energy $d^2$ is a minimal geodesic, which needs the equality cases of V8.5 and of Corollary 10.7) is stated.
Completeness serves only to make a minimal geodesic exist (V7.26); the inequality holds on any $N$.
Minimality is among the paths of $\Omega$, parametrized on $[0, 1]$; by affine reparametrization this is Milnor's notion (V7.24), an equivalence not stated formally.

items.title: Velocity jumps, acceleration and the first variation

milnor.label: §12, p. 71
milnor.statement: For $\omega \in \Omega$, Milnor writes $V_t = d\omega/dt$ for the velocity, $A_t = \frac{D}{dt}\frac{d\omega}{dt}$ for the acceleration, and $\Delta_tV = V_{t^+} - V_{t^-}$ for the discontinuity of the velocity at $t$, which is zero for all but finitely many $t$ in $(0, 1)$.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: for a map $f$ into $V$, the jump $\Delta_tf' = f'(t^+) - f'(t^-)$ is the difference of the right and the left derivative of $f$ at $t$; it vanishes where $f$ is differentiable. Along a path $\omega$, $\frac{DX}{dt}(t) = P_{\omega(t)}X'(t)$, $V = \omega'$ and $A = \frac{D}{dt}V$. The first variation of $\omega$ in the direction $W$ is $-\sum_{0 < t < 1}\langle W_t, \Delta_tV\rangle - \int_0^1\langle W_t, A_t\rangle\,dt$, the sum being finite: for $\omega$ differentiable off a finite set $B$, it is the sum over the points of $B$ in $(0, 1)$. It depends only on $W$ on $[0, 1]$.

diff: The sum is written over all of $(0, 1)$, its terms vanishing off the break points; the formal statement shows it is the finite sum over the break points.

items.title: Calculus on closed strips

milnor.label: §§12–13, pp. 71–76
milnor.statement: The book has no such statement. In the proofs of Theorems 12.2 and 13.1 Milnor differentiates under the integral sign, integrates by parts on each $[t_{i-1}, t_i]$ and adds up, and interchanges partial derivatives of a variation, which is smooth only on closed strips, all without comment.

lean.statement: For $F$ smooth on a closed strip $U \times [a, b]$, $U \subseteq \mathbb R$ open, $a < b$: the partial derivatives $\partial F/\partial u$, $\partial F/\partial t$ computed within the strip are smooth on it, are one-sided $t$-derivatives on the edges, and the mixed partials agree on the whole closed strip, edges included. If $F$ and $F'$ are continuous on the strip and $F'$ is the $u$-derivative of $F$ inside it, then $u \mapsto \int_a^bF(u, t)\,dt$ has derivative $\int_a^bF'(u_0, t)\,dt$ at every $u_0 \in U$, also for integrands that are $C^1$ only piece by piece. If $\int_s^tg = F^-(t) - F^+(s)$ on every piece $[s, t]$ of $[a, b]$ with break points $B$, then $\int_a^bg = F^-(b) - F^+(a) - \sum_{x \in B \cap (a, b)}(F^+(x) - F^-(x))$.

chips: mixed partials up to the edges
diff: These are the analytic facts behind "differentiate under the integral sign" and "integrate by parts on each interval": smoothness on the closed strips, compactness for the domination bound, and the symmetry of second derivatives on the edges, where the $t$-derivatives are one-sided.
The last statement is the bookkeeping by which the boundary terms of the pieces telescope into the jump terms of the first and second variation formulas.

items.title: Theorem 12.2: the first variation formula

milnor.label: §12, Theorem 12.2
milnor.statement: Let $\bar\alpha$ be a variation of $\omega$ with variation field $W$. Then $\frac12\frac{dE(\bar\alpha(u))}{du}\big|_{u=0} = -\sum_t\langle W_t, \Delta_tV\rangle - \int_0^1\langle W_t, A_t\rangle\,dt$. The proof differentiates under the integral sign, uses Lemma 8.3 and "Lemma 8.5" to replace $\frac{D}{\partial u}\frac{\partial\alpha}{\partial t}$ by $\frac{D}{\partial t}\frac{\partial\alpha}{\partial u}$, integrates by parts on each $[t_{i-1}, t_i]$ and adds up.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $\alpha$ be a 1-parameter variation (V8.2) with parameter set $U \subseteq \mathbb R$. For every $u_0 \in U$, $u \mapsto E(\alpha(u, \cdot))$ is differentiable at $u_0$, and $\frac12\frac{d}{du}E(\alpha(u, \cdot))|_{u_0}$ is the first variation (V8.7) of $\alpha(u_0, \cdot)$ in the direction $\frac{\partial\alpha}{\partial u}(u_0, \cdot)$: $$-\sum_t\Big\langle\frac{\partial\alpha}{\partial u}, \Delta_t\frac{\partial\alpha}{\partial t}\Big\rangle - \int_0^1\Big\langle\frac{\partial\alpha}{\partial u}, \frac{D}{\partial t}\frac{\partial\alpha}{\partial t}\Big\rangle\,dt$$ at $(u_0, t)$. At $u_0 = 0$, with $\alpha(0, t) = \omega(t)$ on $[0, 1]$, this is Milnor's formula.

diff: The formula holds at every value of the parameter (the exposition's formula (12.2′)), which is what §13 differentiates; the existence of the derivative is part of the conclusion.

Milnor's reference to Lemma 8.5 should be to Lemma 8.7 (8.5 is the definition of a symmetric connection). The scan loses the leading minus sign of the displayed statement; the end of the proof on p. 72 has it.

Hidden: differentiation under the integral sign and the symmetry of mixed partials on the closed strips (V8.8); the boundary terms telescope into the jump terms because $\partial\alpha/\partial u$ is continuous in $t$.

items.title: Geodesics of $\Omega$, and criticality through the first variation

milnor.label: §12, p. 73
milnor.statement: The path $\omega \in \Omega$ is a geodesic if and only if $\omega$ is $C^\infty$ on the whole interval $[0, 1]$ and its acceleration $\frac{D}{dt}\frac{d\omega}{dt}$ is identically zero along $\omega$. "Clearly" a geodesic is a critical point of $E$.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: a map $\omega$ is an (unbroken) geodesic if it is $C^\infty$ on $[0, 1]$, with one-sided derivatives at the ends, and a geodesic on $(0, 1)$ in the sense of V7.1, so that $A = 0$ there. For $\omega \in \Omega(N; p, q)$: $\omega$ is a critical path (V8.4) iff its first variation (V8.7) vanishes in every direction $W \in T\Omega_\omega$. For a geodesic, the first variation vanishes in every direction.

diff: The acceleration is required to vanish on $(0, 1)$; at the ends it then vanishes by continuity.
The converse direction of "critical iff the first variation vanishes on $T\Omega_\omega$" needs every field to be a variation field, Lemma 11.A (V8.3).

items.title: Corollary 12.3: the critical paths of $E$ are the geodesics

milnor.label: §12, Corollary 12.3
milnor.statement: The path $\omega$ is a critical point for the function $E$ if and only if $\omega$ is a geodesic. Proof: a variation with $W(t) = f(t)A(t)$, $f$ positive except at the $t_i$, gives $A = 0$ on each piece; one with $W(t_i) = \Delta_{t_i}V$ gives $\Delta_{t_i}V = 0$, so $\omega$ is $C^1$; then $\omega$ is $C^\infty$ "from the uniqueness theorem for differential equations".

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: a path $\omega \in \Omega(N; p, q)$ is a critical path of $E$ iff it is a geodesic (V8.10). The steps, for $\omega$ critical and smooth on the pieces of a finite set $B$: the acceleration vanishes at every $t \in (0, 1) \setminus B$; the one-sided velocities and their jumps are tangent to $N$, and every jump $\Delta_tV$, $0 < t < 1$, vanishes; through every $q \in N$ with any $v \in T_qN$ at any time $x$ there is a geodesic on an interval around $x$; and a path that is a geodesic on both sides of $x$, smooth up to $x$ from each side and differentiable at $x$, is a geodesic near $x$.

diff: The test variations exist only by Lemma 11.A (V8.3); $W = fA$ must be continuous at the $t_i$, where the one-sided accelerations differ; and a field with the prescribed values $\Delta_{t_i}V$ has to be constructed. The formal proof uses bump functions at one point at a time.

The last step needs the lift $(\omega, \omega')$ to solve the geodesic equation at the former break point itself (a derivative-extension argument) before uniqueness for the first-order geodesic system (V7.3, V7.4) applies.

items.title: The curvature identity (13.3), and jumps under differentiation

milnor.label: §13, pp. 75–76
milnor.statement: In the proof of Theorem 13.1, the curvature formula $\frac{D}{\partial u_1}\frac{D}{\partial t}V - \frac{D}{\partial t}\frac{D}{\partial u_1}V = R(V, W_1)V$ (Lemma 9.2) and $\frac{D}{\partial u_1}V = \frac{D}{\partial t}W_1$ (Lemma 8.7) give (13.3): $\frac{D}{\partial u_1}\frac{D}{\partial t}V = \frac{D^2W_1}{dt^2} + R(V, W_1)V$. On p. 75 the second term of the differentiated first variation formula is "rearranged", which differentiates the velocity jumps in $u$.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric, $R$ Milnor's curvature tensor with his sign ($0$ off $N$): (i) for $F(u, t)$ smooth on an open subset $O$ of $\mathbb R^2$ with values in $N$, at every point of $O$, $$\frac{D}{\partial u}\frac{D}{\partial t}\frac{\partial F}{\partial t} = \frac{D}{\partial t}\frac{D}{\partial t}\frac{\partial F}{\partial u} + R\Big(\frac{\partial F}{\partial t}, \frac{\partial F}{\partial u}\Big)\frac{\partial F}{\partial t},$$ with $\frac{D}{\partial u}X = P(\partial X/\partial u)$, $\frac{D}{\partial t}X = P(\partial X/\partial t)$. (ii) For a 1-parameter variation $\alpha$, $u_0 \in U$ and $0 < x < 1$, the jump $\Delta_x\frac{\partial\alpha}{\partial t}(u, \cdot)$ is differentiable in $u$ at $u_0$, with derivative $\Delta_x\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\frac{\partial\alpha}{\partial u}(u_0, \cdot)$.

chips: on strips, up to the edges
diff: (i) is (13.3) for a surface, with $x = t$, $y = u$ in Lemma 9.2.

Lemmas 8.7 and 9.2 are applied by Milnor to a surface defined only on strips; Chapter 6 states them for surfaces on all of $\mathbb R^2$, so the identity is proved near interior points, and differentiating a one-sided $t$-derivative in $u$ needs the symmetry of mixed partials on the edges (V8.8).

items.title: Theorem 13.1: the second variation formula

milnor.label: §13, Theorem 13.1
milnor.statement: Let $\bar\alpha : U \to \Omega$ be a 2-parameter variation of the geodesic $\gamma$ with variation fields $W_i = \frac{\partial\bar\alpha}{\partial u_i}(0, 0)$, $i = 1, 2$. Then $$\frac12\frac{\partial^2E(\bar\alpha(u_1, u_2))}{\partial u_1\partial u_2}(0, 0) = -\sum_t\Big\langle W_2(t), \Delta_t\frac{DW_1}{dt}\Big\rangle - \int_0^1\Big\langle W_2, \frac{D^2W_1}{dt^2} + R(V, W_1)V\Big\rangle\,dt.$$ It is introduced on p. 74 to show that $E_{**}$ is well defined, and proved on pp. 75–76 from 12.2, the vanishing of $\Delta_tV$ and $\frac{D}{dt}V$ along a geodesic, (13.2) and (13.3).

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: for a path $\gamma$ with velocity $V$ and fields $W_1, W_2$ along it, let $\Phi(W_1, W_2)$ be the right side above, where $\Delta_t\frac{DW_1}{dt} = P_{\gamma(t)}(\Delta_tW_1')$ is the jump of $\frac{DW_1}{dt} = PW_1'$. Let $\gamma$ be a geodesic (V8.10) and $\alpha(u_1, u_2, t)$ a 2-parameter variation of $\gamma$ ($\alpha(0, 0, t) = \gamma(t)$ on $[0, 1]$) with variation fields $W_1, W_2$. Then $u_1 \mapsto \frac{\partial}{\partial u_2}E(\alpha(u_1, u_2, \cdot))|_{u_2 = 0}$ is differentiable at $u_1 = 0$, with derivative $2\Phi(W_1, W_2)$. Two 2-parameter variations of $\gamma$ whose variation fields agree on $[0, 1]$ give the same value.

diff: Milnor's $\frac{\partial^2E}{\partial u_1\partial u_2}(0, 0)$ is the iterated derivative $\partial/\partial u_1$ of $\partial E/\partial u_2$ along $u_2 = 0$, which is what his proof computes; its existence is part of the conclusion, and $E \circ \bar\alpha$ is not assumed to be of class $C^2$.
The proof needs formula (12.2′) at every $(u_1, 0)$ (V8.9), and differentiation of the jump and integral terms in $u_1$ (V8.8, V8.12).
The scan drops the $-\sum_t$ in front of the first term of the displayed statement; (13.2) on the same page has it.

items.title: The Hessian $E_{**}$

milnor.label: §13, p. 74
milnor.statement: For a geodesic $\gamma$, the Hessian $E_{**} : T\Omega_\gamma \times T\Omega_\gamma \to \mathbb R$ of $E$ at $\gamma$ is defined by analogy with the Hessian $f_{**}$ of a function on a manifold: given $W_1, W_2 \in T\Omega_\gamma$, choose a 2-parameter variation with these variation fields and put $E_{**}(W_1, W_2) = \frac{\partial^2E(\bar\alpha(u_1, u_2))}{\partial u_1\partial u_2}(0, 0)$.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: for $\gamma \in \Omega(N; p, q)$, $E_{**}(W_1, W_2) = 2\Phi(W_1, W_2)$ ($\Phi$ as in V8.13) is a bilinear form on $T\Omega_\gamma$, depending only on the values of the fields on $[0, 1]$. The variation fields of a 2-parameter variation of $\gamma$ lie in $T\Omega_\gamma$. If $\gamma$ is a geodesic, every 2-parameter variation of $\gamma$ with variation fields $W_1, W_2$ has $\frac{\partial^2E}{\partial u_1\partial u_2}(0, 0) = E_{**}(W_1, W_2)$ (in the sense of V8.13), and every pair $W_1, W_2 \in T\Omega_\gamma$ arises (V8.3). So Milnor's definition is well defined and agrees with $E_{**}$.

diff: $\Omega$ has no manifold structure, here as in the book, so $E_{**}$ is defined by the second variation formula and identified with Milnor's definition through variations: every pair of fields comes from a variation (Lemma 11.A), and every such variation computes it (Theorem 13.1).
$E_{**}$ is defined at every $\gamma \in \Omega$; only at a geodesic is it the second derivative of $E$.

items.title: Proposition 13.A: the Hessian as an integral

milnor.label: §13, cf. pp. 75–76
milnor.statement: The book has no such statement; it works throughout with the form of the second variation formula containing $\frac{D^2W_1}{dt^2}$ and the jumps of $\frac{DW_1}{dt}$.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: for $\gamma \in \Omega(N; p, q)$ and $W_1, W_2 \in T\Omega_\gamma$, $$\tfrac12E_{**}(W_1, W_2) = \int_0^1\Big(\Big\langle\frac{DW_1}{dt}, \frac{DW_2}{dt}\Big\rangle - \langle R(V, W_1)V, W_2\rangle\Big)\,dt.$$ $\gamma$ need not be a geodesic.

chips: one integration by parts per piece
used for symmetry and the index
diff: The exposition's Proposition 13.A: one integration by parts on each piece (Lemma 8.3), the boundary terms telescoping into the jump terms, $W_2$ vanishing at the ends.
It carries much of what follows: the symmetry of $E_{**}$ (V8.16), the extension by zero in the index theorem (V9.20), the Poincaré estimate (V9.16) and the test fields of Myers' theorem (V11.11).

items.title: Corollary 13.4: $E_{**}$ is symmetric and bilinear

milnor.label: §13, Corollary 13.4
milnor.statement: The expression $E_{**}(W_1, W_2) = \frac{\partial^2E}{\partial u_1\partial u_2}(0, 0)$ is a well defined, symmetric, bilinear function of $W_1$ and $W_2$: well defined and bilinear by the second variation formula, symmetric because $\frac{\partial^2E}{\partial u_1\partial u_2} = \frac{\partial^2E}{\partial u_2\partial u_1}$.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: for $\gamma \in \Omega(N; p, q)$, $E_{**}$ is a symmetric bilinear form on $T\Omega_\gamma$. For tangent vectors $v, w_1, w_2$ at $x \in N$, $\langle R(v, w_1)v, w_2\rangle = \langle R(v, w_2)v, w_1\rangle$.

diff: Milnor's symmetry argument needs $E \circ \bar\alpha$ of class $C^2$ near $(0, 0)$, which the book does not address. Here symmetry and bilinearity come from the integral form (V8.15) and the symmetry of the curvature term (Lemma 9.3 (4), from the Gauss equation), not from second derivatives; well-definedness is V8.13–V8.14.
Bilinearity in $W_1$ also needs the linearity of $W \mapsto \Delta_t\frac{DW}{dt}$ and $W \mapsto \frac{D^2W}{dt^2}$ on piecewise smooth fields, which the integral form makes unnecessary.

items.title: Remark 13.5: the second derivative along a 1-parameter variation

milnor.label: §13, Remark 13.5
milnor.statement: If $\bar\alpha$ is a 1-parameter variation of the geodesic $\gamma$ with variation field $W$, then $\frac{d^2E(\bar\alpha(u))}{du^2}(0) = E_{**}(W, W)$, by the 2-parameter variation $\beta(u_1, u_2) = \bar\alpha(u_1 + u_2)$.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $\gamma \in \Omega(N; p, q)$ be a geodesic and $\alpha$ a 1-parameter variation of $\gamma$ with variation field $W$. Then $u \mapsto \frac{d}{du}E(\alpha(u, \cdot))$ is differentiable at $0$, and $\frac{d^2E(\bar\alpha(u))}{du^2}(0) = E_{**}(W, W)$.

diff: That $\beta$ is a 2-parameter variation with both variation fields equal to $W$ is checked; the proof is Milnor's, Theorem 13.1 for $\beta$, and the second derivative is shown to exist.

items.title: Lemma 13.6: the Hessian at a minimal geodesic

milnor.label: §13, Lemma 13.6
milnor.statement: If $\gamma$ is a minimal geodesic from $p$ to $q$, then the bilinear pairing $E_{**}$ is positive semi-definite. Hence the index $\lambda$ of $E_{**}$ is zero. Proof: $E(\bar\alpha(u)) \ge E(\gamma) = E(\bar\alpha(0))$ forces $\frac{d^2E(\bar\alpha(u))}{du^2}(0) \ge 0$.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: if $\gamma \in \Omega(N; p, q)$ is a geodesic and is minimal in the sense of V8.6, then $E_{**}(W, W) \ge 0$ for every $W \in T\Omega_\gamma$.

diff: The formal statement is the positive semi-definiteness. The index of a bilinear form is defined only in Chapter 9 (V9.13), and that the index of $E_{**}$ at a minimal geodesic is $0$ is not stated as a theorem.

Only minimality is used, not completeness. That a minimum forces a nonnegative second derivative needs an argument when only the second derivative at $0$ is known to exist: if it were negative, $0$ would also be a local maximum, so the function would be locally constant and its second derivative $0$.

items.title: Linear equations have global solutions (Lemma 14.A)

milnor.label: §14, p. 77
milnor.statement: The Jacobi equation, a linear second-order differential equation, has $2n$ linearly independent solutions, each of which is "defined throughout $\gamma$" and of class $C^\infty$; a Jacobi field is determined by its initial conditions $J(0)$ and $\frac{DJ}{dt}(0)$. Milnor gives no proof.

lean.statement: Let $E$ be a complete real normed space and $t \mapsto A(t)$ a continuous map from $\mathbb R$ to the continuous linear maps $E \to E$. (i) For every $t_0 \in \mathbb R$ and $x_0 \in E$ the equation $x' = A(t)x$ has a solution on all of $\mathbb R$ with $x(t_0) = x_0$, and the solution with value $\xi$ at $s$ depends linearly on $\xi$. (ii) If $a < b$ and $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$ and solves the equation on $(a, b)$, then for every $s \in [a, b]$, end points included, $f$ agrees on $[a, b]$ with the solution whose value at $s$ is $f(s)$. (iii) If $A$ is $C^\infty$ on $[a, b]$ (one-sided derivatives at the ends) and $f'(t) = A(t)f(t)$ at every $t \in [a, b]$, then $f$ is $C^\infty$ on $[a, b]$.

diff: The book asserts global solutions without proof; the local existence theorem gives solutions only on intervals of length about $1/\sup\|A\|$, so a global theorem for linear equations is needed. It is proved by truncating the equation radially and bounding the solution by Grönwall's inequality in both time directions, so that the truncation is never active.
The coefficients may be any continuous family on any complete space, extending the skew-adjoint case of Chapter 6.

items.title: Jacobi fields and the Jacobi system

milnor.label: §14, p. 77
milnor.statement: A vector field $J$ along a geodesic $\gamma$ is a *Jacobi field* if it satisfies the Jacobi differential equation $\frac{D^2J}{dt^2} + R(V, J)V = 0$, $V = d\gamma/dt$. In terms of orthonormal parallel fields $P_1, \dots, P_n$ along $\gamma$, writing $J = \sum f^iP_i$, it becomes a linear system with coefficients $\langle R(V, P_j)V, P_i\rangle$; a Jacobi field is completely determined by its initial conditions $J(0)$ and $\frac{DJ}{dt}(0)$.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric. A *smooth curve in $N$ on $[0, 1]$* is a map $\gamma : \mathbb R \to V$ that is $C^\infty$ on $[0, 1]$, with one-sided derivatives at the ends, and has values in $N$ there; every geodesic of $\Omega$ is one. A map $J$ is a *Jacobi field along $\gamma$* if it is $C^\infty$ on $[0, 1]$, tangent along $\gamma$, and $\frac{D^2J}{dt^2} + R(V, J)V = 0$ on $(0, 1)$, $D/dt$ the covariant derivative of V8.7. With $S = P'P - PP'$ and $K(t)v = R(V, P(t)v)V$, the Jacobi system is the linear system $J' = SJ + Y$, $Y' = SY - KJ$ for $(J, Y)$ in $V \times V$; its solution with any value at any time exists on $\mathbb R$. If $s \in [0, 1]$ and both initial values are tangent at $\gamma(s)$, both components stay tangent on $[0, 1]$, the first is a Jacobi field and the second its covariant derivative. Conversely every Jacobi field $J$ agrees on $[0, 1]$ with the solution whose value at $s$ is $(J(s), \frac{DJ}{dt}(s))$; in particular $J(s) = 0$ and $\frac{DJ}{dt}(s) = 0$ force $J = 0$ on $[0, 1]$.

chips: no parallel frame: a system in $V \times V$
diff: No frame is used: the unknown is $(J, \frac{DJ}{dt})$ in $V \times V$, and the term $S$ keeps solutions with tangent initial values tangent, their normal parts solving a homogeneous linear system and vanishing at $s$.
Parallel frames along $\gamma$ (Lemma 8.2) are formalized only for curves on all of $\mathbb R$; the frame-free system avoids extending $\gamma$.
The definition and the solution theory hold along any smooth curve in $N$, not only along a geodesic, with initial values at any $s \in [0, 1]$; the global existence is V9.1.

items.title: The space of Jacobi fields (Corollary 14.B)

milnor.label: §14, p. 77
milnor.statement: The Jacobi equation has $2n$ linearly independent solutions, and a Jacobi field is completely determined by $J(0)$ and $\frac{DJ}{dt}(0)$.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $\gamma$ be a smooth curve in $N$ on $[0, 1]$ (V9.2) and $n = \dim N$. $\mathcal J(\gamma)$ is the vector space of the Jacobi fields along $\gamma$ that are constant off $[0, 1]$; every Jacobi field agrees on $[0, 1]$ with one of them. For every $s \in [0, 1]$, $J \mapsto (J(s), \frac{DJ}{dt}(s))$ is a linear isomorphism $\mathcal J(\gamma) \to T_{\gamma(s)}N \times T_{\gamma(s)}N$: every pair of tangent vectors at $\gamma(s)$ is the value and covariant derivative at $s$ of exactly one field of $\mathcal J(\gamma)$; and $\dim\mathcal J(\gamma) = 2n$.

diff: The isomorphism holds at every $s \in [0, 1]$, along any smooth curve in $N$; that every pair of initial values occurs is the global existence of V9.1.
Fields are normalized to be constant off $[0, 1]$, so that the space is finite-dimensional on the nose; its elements are maps on $\mathbb R$.

items.title: Conjugate points and their multiplicity

milnor.label: §14, p. 77
milnor.statement: For $a \ne b$, the points $p = \gamma(a)$ and $q = \gamma(b)$ are *conjugate* along $\gamma$ if there is a non-zero Jacobi field $J$ along $\gamma$ which vanishes for $t = a$ and $t = b$; the multiplicity of $p$ and $q$ as conjugate points is the dimension of the vector space of all such fields. A footnote warns that if $\gamma$ has self-intersections one should rather say that the parameter values $a$ and $b$ are conjugate.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $\gamma$ be a smooth curve in $N$ on $[0, 1]$. Parameters $a$ and $b$ are *conjugate along $\gamma$* if $a, b \in [0, 1]$, $a \ne b$, and some Jacobi field along $\gamma$ vanishes at $a$ and at $b$ without vanishing identically on $[0, 1]$. Their *multiplicity* is the dimension of the space of fields of $\mathcal J(\gamma)$ vanishing at $a$ and $b$, finite by V9.3; for $a \ne b$ in $[0, 1]$ they are conjugate iff the multiplicity is positive.

diff: Conjugacy is a relation between parameter values, as Milnor's footnote recommends; throughout §15, "the conjugate points $\gamma(t)$" are read as the conjugate parameters $t$.

items.title: Theorem 14.1: the null vectors of $E_{**}$ are the Jacobi fields

milnor.label: §14, Theorem 14.1
milnor.statement: A vector field $W_1 \in T\Omega_\gamma$ belongs to the null space of $E_{**}$ if and only if $W_1$ is a Jacobi field. Proof (pp. 78–79): a Jacobi field vanishing at the ends is null by the second variation formula; conversely, testing against $W_2 = f(t)(\frac{D^2W_1}{dt^2} + R(V, W_1)V)$, $f$ vanishing exactly at the break points, makes $W_1$ a Jacobi field on each piece, testing against a field with values $\Delta_{t_i}\frac{DW_1}{dt}$ at the break points removes the jumps, and the pieces "fit together" since a solution is determined by $W_1(t_i)$ and $\frac{DW_1}{dt}(t_i)$.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $\gamma \in \Omega(N; p, q)$ be a geodesic (V8.10) and $W_1 \in T\Omega_\gamma$. Then $E_{**}(W_1, W_2) = 0$ for every $W_2 \in T\Omega_\gamma$ iff $W_1$ is a Jacobi field along $\gamma$; in particular such a $W_1$ is $C^\infty$ on all of $[0, 1]$. On the way: for a Jacobi field $J$ along any curve, $\Phi(J, Y) = 0$ for every field $Y$; for a null vector the Jacobi operator vanishes off the break points and every jump of $W_1'$ is tangent and zero; and for a smooth tangent field the Jacobi equation is a second-order equation in $V$.

chips: pieces joined by a local argument
diff: In $V$, the absence of jumps of $\frac{DW_1}{dt} = PW_1'$ makes $W_1$ of class $C^1$ only because the normal parts of the two one-sided derivatives agree (both are $\mathrm{II}(V, W_1)$).

The test field with prescribed values at the break points has to be constructed, and Milnor's fitting together needs Jacobi fields along all of $\gamma$ with given initial values (V9.2), stated in the book without proof. The formal proof joins the pieces by a local argument instead: a smooth second-order equation holds on both sides of a former break point with a right side continuous across it.

items.title: Theorem 14.1: the null space and the nullity

milnor.label: §14, Theorem 14.1, pp. 77–79
milnor.statement: The null space of $E_{**}$ is the space of $W_1 \in T\Omega_\gamma$ with $E_{**}(W_1, W_2) = 0$ for all $W_2$, the nullity $\nu$ is its dimension, and $E_{**}$ is degenerate if $\nu > 0$ (pp. 77–78). Theorem 14.1 continues: hence $E_{**}$ is degenerate if and only if the end points $p$ and $q$ are conjugate along $\gamma$, and the nullity of $E_{**}$ equals their multiplicity as conjugate points. On p. 79: the nullity is always finite.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: for $\gamma \in \Omega(N; p, q)$, the *null space* of $E_{**}$ is the space of the restrictions to $[0, 1]$, extended as constants, of the $W_1 \in T\Omega_\gamma$ with $E_{**}(W_1, W_2) = 0$ for all $W_2 \in T\Omega_\gamma$, and the *nullity* is its dimension. If $\gamma$ is a geodesic, the null space is the space of fields of $\mathcal J(\gamma)$ vanishing at $0$ and $1$; so the nullity is the multiplicity of $0$ and $1$ as conjugate parameters (V9.4), in particular finite, and it is positive iff $0$ and $1$ are conjugate along $\gamma$.

diff: Fields are maps on $\mathbb R$ whose values off $[0, 1]$ play no role, so the literal kernel of the formal $E_{**}$ contains every field vanishing on $[0, 1]$ and is infinite-dimensional; the null space is therefore taken modulo the values off $[0, 1]$.
Finiteness needs the identification with a subspace of the $2n$-dimensional $\mathcal J(\gamma)$ (V9.3).

items.title: Remark 14.2: the nullity is less than $n$

milnor.label: §14, Remark 14.2
milnor.statement: Actually the nullity satisfies $0 \le \nu < n$: the Jacobi fields vanishing for $t = 0$ form a space of dimension precisely $n$, and $J_t = tV_t$ is a Jacobi field vanishing for $t = 0$ but not for $t = 1$.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: along a smooth curve $\gamma$ in $N$ on $[0, 1]$, the fields of $\mathcal J(\gamma)$ vanishing at $0$ form a space of dimension $n = \dim N$. If $\gamma$ is moreover a geodesic on $(0, 1)$, then $t \mapsto tV(t)$ is a Jacobi field, and $\gamma$ is constant on $[0, 1]$ if $V(1) = 0$; along a constant curve, $t \mapsto ty$ is a Jacobi field for every tangent vector $y$. Hence, for a geodesic $\gamma \in \Omega(N; p, q)$ and $n \ge 1$, the nullity of $E_{**}$ satisfies $\nu < n$.

diff: Milnor's $J_1 = V_1 \ne 0$ requires $\gamma$ non-constant; the formal statement includes the constant geodesic ($p = q$), with $ty$, $y \ne 0$, in place of $tV$.
$\nu < n$ requires $n \ge 1$: for $n = 0$, $\nu = 0 = n$.

items.title: Example 1: no conjugate points in a flat space

milnor.label: §14, Example 1
milnor.statement: Suppose that $M$ is "flat", in the sense that the curvature tensor is identically zero. Then the Jacobi equation becomes $\frac{D^2J}{dt^2} = 0$; in parallel fields, $J = \sum f^iP_i$ with $\frac{d^2f^i}{dt^2} = 0$. Evidently a Jacobi field along $\gamma$ can have at most one zero; thus there are no conjugate points, and $E_{**}$ is non-degenerate.

lean.statement: Let $N \subseteq V$ be a slice submanifold every tangent space of which is all of $V$ (for instance an open subset of $V$, which is a slice submanifold of codimension $0$). Then the induced metric is flat ($R = 0$); along a curve in $N$ every Jacobi field is affine, $J(t) = J(0) + t(J(1) - J(0))$ on $[0, 1]$; no two parameters are conjugate along any curve in $N$; and at every geodesic of $\Omega(N; p, q)$ the index and the nullity of $E_{**}$ are $0$.

diff: The verified Chapter 9 lists Example 1 as not formalized; the case proved, in `Morse/Chapter10/Incomplete.lean`, is the one Chapter 10 needs for its counterexample to Corollary 17.5 (V10.27).

Milnor's hypothesis is $R \equiv 0$; the formal one is that $N$ has codimension $0$. A flat manifold embedded with positive codimension, such as a flat torus in $\mathbb R^4$, has $R = 0$ but is not covered, since its Jacobi fields are not computed without parallel frames.
The formal statement also gives index $0$ at every geodesic, which Milnor does not state here.

items.title: Example 2: antipodal points of $S^n$

milnor.label: §14, Example 2, pp. 79–80
milnor.statement: Suppose that $p$ and $q$ are antipodal points on the unit sphere $S^n$, and let $\gamma$ be a great circle arc from $p$ to $q$. Then $p$ and $q$ are conjugate with multiplicity $n - 1$, so the nullity of $E_{**}$ takes its largest possible value. Proof (p. 80): rotating the sphere about the axis through $p$ and $q$ gives variations through geodesics, whose variation fields are Jacobi fields vanishing at $p$ and $q$ (Lemma 14.3); rotating in $n - 1$ different directions gives $n - 1$ linearly independent ones.

lean.statement: On the unit sphere $S^n \subseteq \mathbb R^{n+1}$, $n \ge 1$, with the induced metric: for unit vectors $p \perp u$ and $L \in \mathbb R$, $c(t) = \cos(Lt)\,p + \sin(Lt)\,u$ is a geodesic on $\mathbb R$; for every $e \perp p, u$, $t \mapsto \sin(Lt)\,e$ is a Jacobi field along $c$; and for $L > 0$ and $0 < t \le 1$, the multiplicity of $0$ and $t$ as conjugate parameters along $c$ is $n - 1$ if $Lt$ is a multiple of $\pi$, and $0$ otherwise. For $L = \pi$, $t = 1$ this is Milnor's statement for the great semicircle from $p$ to $-p$.

diff: The verified Chapter 9 lists Example 2 as not formalized; it is proved in `Morse/Chapter10/SphereGeodesics.lean`, where the index of every geodesic between two points of $S^n$ is computed (V10.23).

The formal statement covers every great circle and every parameter: the conjugate parameters along $c$ are exactly the $t$ with $Lt \in \pi\mathbb Z$, each of multiplicity $n - 1$, which is what the index computation of §17 needs.

The Jacobi fields are checked directly with $R(x, y)z = \langle x, z\rangle y - \langle y, z\rangle x$ rather than through rotations and Lemma 14.3; the upper bound $n - 1$ comes from Remark 14.2 (V9.7), as in the book.

items.title: Lemma 14.3: variations through geodesics give Jacobi fields

milnor.label: §14, Lemma 14.3
milnor.statement: A variation of $\gamma$ through geodesics, not necessarily keeping the end points fixed, is a $C^\infty$ map $\alpha : (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \times [0, 1] \to M$ with $\alpha(0, t) = \gamma(t)$ and each $\bar\alpha(u)$ a geodesic (p. 79). Lemma 14.3: its variation vector field $W(t) = \frac{\partial\alpha}{\partial u}(0, t)$ is a Jacobi field along $\gamma$. Proof: apply $\frac{D}{\partial u}$ to $\frac{D}{\partial t}\frac{\partial\alpha}{\partial t} = 0$ and use Lemmas 9.2 and 8.7.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $\varepsilon > 0$ and $\alpha(u, t)$ be $C^\infty$ on $(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \times [0, 1]$ (one-sided derivatives along the edges $t = 0, 1$), with values in $N$ there, such that each $t \mapsto \alpha(u, t)$, $|u| < \varepsilon$, is a geodesic on $(0, 1)$. Then $W(t) = \frac{\partial\alpha}{\partial u}(0, t)$ is a Jacobi field along $\alpha(0, \cdot)$. Being a Jacobi field along $\gamma$ depends only on $\gamma$ on $[0, 1]$.

diff: Lemmas 9.2 and 8.7 are applied to a map defined on a strip and smooth up to its edges; the formal proof uses the identity (13.3) of V8.12 on the open strip, and gets the smoothness of $W$ up to $t = 0, 1$ from that of $\alpha$ on the closed strip.

items.title: Lemma 14.4: every Jacobi field comes from a variation through geodesics

milnor.label: §14, Lemma 14.4
milnor.statement: Every Jacobi field along a geodesic $\gamma : [0, 1] \to M$ may be obtained by a variation of $\gamma$ through geodesics. Proof: in a neighbourhood $U$ of $\gamma(0)$ where any two points are joined by a unique minimal geodesic depending differentiably on the end points, with $\gamma(t) \in U$ for $0 \le t \le \delta$, minimal geodesics between the points of two curves $a(u)$, $b(u)$ give Jacobi fields along $\gamma|[0, \delta]$ with arbitrary values at $0$ and $\delta$; so $J \mapsto (J(0), J(\delta))$ is onto, hence an isomorphism (both spaces have dimension $2n$); "using the compactness of $[0, 1]$", the geodesics extend over $[0, 1]$ for small $u$.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: (i) for $x_1 \in N$ and $R > 0$ there are an open $U \ni x_1$, an $h > 0$ and $\Phi$, $C^\infty$ on $U \times \{\|w\| < R\} \times (-h, h)$, with $\exp_y(tw) = \Phi(y, w, t)$ a geodesic on $(-h, h)$ for $y \in N \cap U$, $w \in T_yN$, $\|w\| < R$. (ii) A smooth curve $\gamma$ in $N$ on $[0, 1]$ that is a geodesic on $(0, 1)$ agrees on $[0, 1]$ with $t \mapsto \exp_{\gamma(0)}(tV(0))$, a geodesic on an open interval containing $[0, 1]$. (iii) Geodesics $t \mapsto \exp_{c(u)}(t\,w(u))$ with smooth initial data depend smoothly on $(u, t)$ over any compact time interval on which the one at $u = 0$ exists. (iv) **Lemma 14.4:** for such a $\gamma$ and a Jacobi field $J$ along it, there are $\varepsilon > 0$ and $\alpha$ satisfying the hypotheses of Lemma 14.3 (V9.8) on $(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \times [0, 1]$, with $\alpha(0, t) = \gamma(t)$ and $\frac{\partial\alpha}{\partial u}(0, t) = J(t)$ for $t \in [0, 1]$.

chips: geodesic segments extend past the ends
diff: The statement is Milnor's; the proof departs from his. The variation is built from initial data, $\alpha(u, t) = \exp_{c(u)}(t\,w(u))$ with $c(u) = \exp_{\gamma(0)}(uJ(0))$ and $w(u) = P_{c(u)}(V(0) + u\frac{DJ}{dt}(0))$; its variation field is a Jacobi field with the initial data of $J$, hence equals $J$ (V9.2). No minimal geodesic, restriction to $[0, \delta]$ or dimension count is used.

Milnor's construction returns $\bar\alpha(0) = \gamma|[0, \delta]$ only if $\gamma|[0, \delta]$ is *the* minimal geodesic between its ends, which $\gamma([0, \delta]) \subseteq U$ does not say; it is true for his $U$ by an argument the book omits. His compactness step is the smooth dependence of geodesics on initial data over a compact interval, (iii), with the openness of the domain of $\exp$ — neither among the statements of §10.
(ii) is the extension of a geodesic segment past its end points, which makes Milnor's domain of $\exp$ equal to the formal one (V7.7).

items.title: A Jacobi field is determined by its values at two non-conjugate points

milnor.label: §14, p. 81
milnor.statement: In the proof of Lemma 14.4, in parentheses and without proof: more generally a Jacobi field is determined by its values at any two non-conjugate points.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $\gamma$ be a smooth curve in $N$ on $[0, 1]$ and $a \ne b$ in $[0, 1]$ parameters that are not conjugate along $\gamma$ (V9.4). Then $J \mapsto (J(a), J(b))$ is a linear isomorphism $\mathcal J(\gamma) \to T_{\gamma(a)}N \times T_{\gamma(b)}N$: a Jacobi field is determined by its values at $a$ and $b$, and these values can be prescribed.

diff: Injectivity is the definition of non-conjugacy; the formal statement adds surjectivity, by the dimension count of V9.3.

items.title: Remark 14.5: Jacobi fields along short geodesics

milnor.label: §14, Remark 14.5
milnor.statement: The argument of Lemma 14.4 shows that in any such neighbourhood $U$ the Jacobi fields along a geodesic segment in $U$ are uniquely determined by their values at the end points of the segment.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: (i) let $\varepsilon$ be a normal radius at $q \in N$ (V7.9), $v \in T_qN$ and $\|v\| < \varepsilon$. Then $\sigma(t) = \exp_q(tv)$ is a smooth curve in $N$ on $[0, 1]$; a Jacobi field along $\sigma$ vanishing at $t = 0$ and $t = 1$ vanishes on $[0, 1]$; and $J \mapsto (J(0), J(1))$ is a linear isomorphism $\mathcal J(\sigma) \to T_qN \times T_{\sigma(1)}N$. (ii) Every $p \in N$ has an open neighbourhood $O$ in $V$, with an $\varepsilon > 0$, such that for all $q_1, q_2 \in N \cap O$ there is $v \in T_{q_1}N$ with $\|v\| < \varepsilon$ and $\exp_{q_1}(v) = q_2$, $\varepsilon$ is a normal radius at $q_1$, and a Jacobi field along $t \mapsto \exp_{q_1}(tv)$ vanishing at both ends vanishes on $[0, 1]$.

diff: Milnor's $U$ (unique minimal geodesics depending differentiably on their ends) is replaced by the neighbourhoods of Lemma 10.3 (V7.10), and "a geodesic segment in $U$" by $t \mapsto \exp_{q_1}(tv)$ with $\|v\|$ below a normal radius, the shortest path of V7.15.

Injectivity comes from the local inverse of $\exp_q$: the Jacobi field with $J(0) = 0$, $\frac{DJ}{dt}(0) = w$ is $t \mapsto d(\exp_q)_{tv}(tw)$, and $d(\exp_q)_v$ is injective; surjectivity is the dimension count. Milnor goes the other way, from the surjectivity of his construction.

items.title: Remark 14.6: no conjugate points near the start

milnor.label: §14, Remark 14.6
milnor.statement: The proof of 14.4 also shows that there is a neighbourhood $(-\delta, \delta)$ of $0$ such that $\gamma(t)$ is not conjugate to $\gamma(0)$ along $\gamma$ for $t \in (-\delta, \delta)$; and, by 15.2, the points conjugate to $\gamma(0)$ along an entire geodesic have no cluster points.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: for every smooth curve $\gamma$ in $N$ on $[0, 1]$ there is $\delta > 0$ such that no $t \in (0, \delta)$ is conjugate to $0$ along $\gamma$.

chips: no statement along an entire geodesic
diff: Only $t > 0$, $\gamma$ being given on $[0, 1]$; the statement that the conjugate points along an entire geodesic have no cluster points is not formalized (the reparametrization of a geodesic to $[0, 1]$, the exposition's Lemma 14.C, is not formalized).

It holds along any smooth curve in $N$, with $\delta$ the explicit mesh of V9.16, since no two parameters closer than it are conjugate; Milnor's neighbourhood $U$, which needs $\gamma|[0, t]$ to be the minimal geodesic between its ends, is not used.

items.title: The index and the nullity of a bilinear form

milnor.label: §15, p. 83; §2, p. 5
milnor.statement: The index $\lambda$ of $E_{**}$ is the maximum dimension of a subspace of $T\Omega_\gamma$ on which $E_{**}$ is negative definite (p. 83); for a bilinear functional on a vector space, the index and the nullity are defined in §2 (p. 5).

lean.statement: Let $B$ be a bilinear form on a real vector space $X$. $B$ is negative (positive) definite on a subspace $S$ if $B(x, x) < 0$ ($> 0$) for every $x \ne 0$ in $S$. The *index* of $B$ is the supremum, in $\{0, 1, 2, \dots\} \cup \{\infty\}$, of the dimensions of the finite-dimensional subspaces on which $B$ is negative definite; a finite index is the dimension of such a subspace. A linear map $L$ with $B'(Lx, Ly) = B(x, y)$ does not decrease the index, so an isomorphism carrying $B$ to $B'$ preserves it; on a finite-dimensional space the index is Mathlib's negative index of inertia of $x \mapsto B(x, x)$. The *nullity* is the dimension of $\{x : B(x, y) = 0 \text{ for all } y\}$; for $E_{**}$ the null space is read on $[0, 1]$ (V9.6).

diff: Milnor's "maximum dimension" presupposes that the maximum exists; here the index is a supremum over finite-dimensional subspaces, possibly $\infty$, and its finiteness for $E_{**}$ is part of Theorem 15.1, as in the book. A negative definite subspace of infinite dimension contains finite-dimensional ones of every dimension, and so also gives $\infty$.

items.title: Linear algebra for the index theorem (Lemmas 15.A and 15.B)

milnor.label: §15, pp. 85–87
milnor.statement: The book has no such statements; on pp. 85–87 Milnor uses without proof: that the index and nullity of $E_{**}$ can be computed on a summand complementary to a perpendicular subspace on which $E_{**}$ is positive definite ("the proof is straightforward", Lemma 15.4); that definiteness of $H_\tau$ on a subspace persists for $H_{\tau'}$ near $H_\tau$; a positive definite subspace of dimension $ni - \lambda(\tau) - \nu$; and a compound matrix that is "certainly negative definite" for small $c$.

diff: These are stated and proved as lemmas. In (5) the hidden point is that a negative definite Gram matrix makes the $\lambda + \nu$ fields linearly independent; (3) is proved by the compactness of the unit sphere of $S$, and (5) from (3) for the family $Ua + c^{-1}Jb - cYb$.

items.title: The second variation formula for piecewise Jacobi fields

milnor.label: §15, pp. 84 and 87
milnor.statement: In the proof of Lemma 15.3 (p. 84), for a broken Jacobi field $W_1$ and a field $W_2$ vanishing at the break points, the second variation formula reduces to its jump terms; on p. 87 the values of $E_{**}(J_h, \cdot)$ are seen "easily" from the second variation formula.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $\gamma \in \Omega(N; p, q)$, $X, Y \in T\Omega_\gamma$, and $B$ a finite set such that near every $t \in (0, 1) \setminus B$ the field $X$ agrees with some Jacobi field along $\gamma$ (the zero field is one). Then $$E_{**}(X, Y) = -2\sum_{b \in B \cap (0, 1)}\Big\langle Y(b), \Delta_b\frac{DX}{dt}\Big\rangle,$$ $\Delta_b\frac{DX}{dt} = P_{\gamma(b)}(\Delta_bX')$. $\gamma$ need not be a geodesic.

diff: The reduction that Milnor performs twice inside proofs is stated once: the integrand of the second variation formula (V8.13) vanishes off the finite set $B \cup \{1\}$.

items.title: Positivity near zeros, and fine subdivisions

milnor.label: §15, pp. 83–84
milnor.statement: Each $\gamma(t)$ lies in an open set $U$ in which any two points are joined by a unique minimal geodesic depending differentiably on the end points (§10), and the subdivision $0 = t_0 < t_1 < \dots < t_k = 1$ is chosen "sufficiently fine" that each $\gamma|[t_{i-1}, t_i]$ lies in such a $U$ and is minimal. Milnor uses two consequences: along each segment the Jacobi fields are determined by their end values, which can be prescribed (Remark 14.5); and each segment has smaller energy than any other path between its end points (p. 84).

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $\gamma$ be a smooth curve in $N$ on $[0, 1]$, $C \ge 0$ a bound for $\|P'(t)\|^2 + \|K(t)\|$ on $[0, 1]$ ($K$ as in V9.2), and $h_0 = 1/(C + 1)$. (i) *Poincaré estimate:* if $X \in T\Omega_\gamma$ and every $t \in [0, 1]$ has a zero $s \in [0, t]$ of $X$ with $t - s \le h_0$, then $\int_0^1\|X\|^2\,dt \le \frac12E_{**}(X, X)$; so $E_{**}(X, X) \le 0$ forces $X = 0$ on $[0, 1]$. (ii) If $0 \le a < b \le 1$ and $b - a \le h_0$, a field of $\mathcal J(\gamma)$ vanishing at $a$ and $b$ is $0$, and $J \mapsto (J(a), J(b))$ is an isomorphism onto $T_{\gamma(a)}N \times T_{\gamma(b)}N$: no two parameters at distance at most $h_0$ are conjugate. (iii) A finite set $B \subseteq (0, \tau)$ is *fine for $[0, \tau]$* if consecutive points of $\{0\} \cup B \cup \{\tau\}$ are at most $h_0$ apart; for every $\tau > 0$ there is one whose last point is within $h_0/2$ of $\tau$.

diff: "Sufficiently fine" becomes the explicit mesh $h_0$, which depends only on bounds for $P'$ and the curvature along $\gamma$; $\gamma$ need not be a geodesic, and neither $\exp$ nor minimal geodesics enter.

The existence of Milnor's subdivisions needs a Lebesgue number of a finite cover and a length bound for minimality (Theorem 10.4), which the book does not spell out; the Poincaré estimate replaces both of his uses.

items.title: Broken Jacobi fields and $T'$

milnor.label: §15, pp. 83–84 and 86
milnor.statement: $T\Omega_\gamma(t_0, t_1, \dots, t_k)$ is the space of vector fields $W$ along $\gamma$ vanishing at $0$ and $1$ such that each $W|[t_{i-1}, t_i]$ is a Jacobi field along $\gamma|[t_{i-1}, t_i]$: a finite-dimensional space of broken Jacobi fields (p. 83). $T'$ is the space of fields with $W(t_0) = W(t_1) = \dots = W(t_k) = 0$, and "it follows from §14.5" that the broken Jacobi field with given values at the $t_i$ exists and is unique (p. 84). On p. 86, along $\gamma_\tau$, the broken Jacobi fields for $0 < t_1 < \dots < t_i < \tau$ form a space isomorphic to $TM_{\gamma(t_1)} \oplus \dots \oplus TM_{\gamma(t_i)}$.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $\gamma$ be a smooth curve in $N$ on $[0, 1]$. For $\tau \in \mathbb R$, the fields along $\gamma|[0, \tau]$ are the fields of $T\Omega_\gamma$ vanishing outside $[0, \tau]$. Let $0 < \tau \le 1$ and $B$ be fine for $[0, \tau]$ (V9.16). A map is a *broken Jacobi field* on $[0, \tau]$ for $B$ if on each piece between consecutive points of $\{0\} \cup B \cup \{\tau\}$ it agrees with a field of $\mathcal J(\gamma)$. Milnor's $T\Omega_\gamma(t_0, \dots, t_k)$ is the space of fields along $\gamma|[0, \tau]$ that are broken Jacobi fields, and $T'$ the fields along $\gamma|[0, \tau]$ vanishing at the points of $B$. $W \mapsto (W(b))_{b \in B}$ is a linear isomorphism from the broken Jacobi fields onto $\bigoplus_{b \in B}T_{\gamma(b)}N$.

diff: Everything is along $\gamma|[0, \tau]$ for every $\tau \in (0, 1]$, as fields on $[0, 1]$ vanishing outside $[0, \tau]$; Milnor uses $\tau = 1$ here and $\gamma_\tau$ on p. 86.

A piece is the restriction of a Jacobi field along all of $\gamma$, which is equivalent to being a Jacobi field along the segment by V9.1–V9.2, an equivalence not stated formally. Existence is by induction over the division points with V9.16 (ii); Milnor's "follows from §14.5" also needs the gluing of the pieces.

items.title: Lemma 15.3: the splitting of $T\Omega_\gamma$

milnor.label: §15, Lemma 15.3
milnor.statement: $T\Omega_\gamma = T\Omega_\gamma(t_0, \dots, t_k) \oplus T'$, the two subspaces are mutually perpendicular with respect to $E_{**}$, and $E_{**}$ restricted to $T'$ is positive definite. Proof (pp. 84–85): $W = W_1 + (W - W_1)$; perpendicularity from the second variation formula; $E_{**}(W, W) \ge 0$ on $T'$ because each segment is minimal, and $E_{**}(W, W) = 0$ puts $W$ in the null space, so $W$ is a Jacobi field, and $T'$ contains no Jacobi field other than $0$.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $\gamma$ be a smooth curve in $N$ on $[0, 1]$, $0 < \tau \le 1$ and $B$ fine for $[0, \tau]$. (i) The fields along $\gamma|[0, \tau]$ are the direct sum of the broken Jacobi fields and $T'$ (V9.17). (ii) For a broken Jacobi field $W_1$ and every field $Y$ along $\gamma|[0, \tau]$, $E_{**}(W_1, Y) = -2\sum_{b \in B}\langle Y(b), \Delta_b\frac{DW_1}{dt}\rangle$; in particular $E_{**}(W_1, W_2) = 0$ for $W_2 \in T'$. (iii) $E_{**}(W, W) > 0$ for every $W \ne 0$ in $T'$.

diff: Stated along $\gamma|[0, \tau]$ for every $\tau \in (0, 1]$, for fine subdivisions in the sense of V9.16; Milnor's lemma is $\tau = 1$ for his subdivisions.

(iii) departs from Milnor's proof: a field of $T'$ has a zero within $h_0$ before every point, so the Poincaré estimate gives $E_{**}(W, W) > 0$ directly, without minimal geodesics, variations or Theorem 14.1.

items.title: Lemma 15.4: the index on the broken Jacobi fields

milnor.label: §15, Lemma 15.4
milnor.statement: The index (or the nullity) of $E_{**}$ is equal to the index (or the nullity) of $E_{**}$ restricted to the space $T\Omega_\gamma(t_0, \dots, t_k)$ of broken Jacobi fields; in particular the index $\lambda$ is always finite. Milnor adds only that "the proof is straightforward".

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $\gamma$, $\tau$ and $B$ be as in V9.18. The index (V9.13) of $E_{**}$ on the fields along $\gamma|[0, \tau]$ equals its index on the broken Jacobi fields; the null space of $E_{**}$ on the fields along $\gamma|[0, \tau]$ is the null space of its restriction to the broken Jacobi fields, and the latter has dimension $\nu(\tau)$, the multiplicity of $0$ and $\tau$ (V9.4), because a broken Jacobi field without jumps agrees on $[0, \tau]$ with a single field of $\mathcal J(\gamma)$. In particular the index is at most the dimension of the broken Jacobi fields, hence finite, for every $\tau \in (0, 1]$.

diff: The "straightforward" proof is the abstract Lemma 15.B (V9.14 (4)) applied to Lemma 15.3.
Stated along $\gamma|[0, \tau]$ (Milnor states $\tau = 1$ and applies it to $\gamma_\tau$ on p. 86), for subdivisions fine in the sense of V9.16; the theorem needs only one fine subdivision.
The nullity on the broken Jacobi fields is identified with $\nu(\tau)$ directly; Milnor gets this on p. 86 from Theorem 14.1 for $\gamma_\tau$.

items.title: $\lambda(\tau)$, and Assertions (1) and (2)

milnor.label: §15, p. 85
milnor.statement: For $0 < \tau \le 1$, let $\gamma_\tau = \gamma|[0, \tau]$, a geodesic from $\gamma(0)$ to $\gamma(\tau)$, and let $\lambda(\tau)$ be the index of the associated Hessian $(E_0^\tau)_{**}$; so $\lambda(1)$ is the index we are trying to compute. Assertion (1): $\lambda(\tau)$ is a monotone function of $\tau$, because a field along $\gamma_\tau$ vanishing at both ends extends by zero to one along $\gamma_{\tau'}$. Assertion (2): $\lambda(\tau) = 0$ for small $\tau$, because $\gamma_\tau$ is then a minimal geodesic (Lemma 13.6).

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: for a smooth curve $\gamma$ in $N$ on $[0, 1]$ and $\tau \in \mathbb R$, $\lambda(\tau)$ is the index of $E_{**}$ (of $\gamma$ on $[0, 1]$) restricted to the fields along $\gamma|[0, \tau]$, i.e. vanishing outside $[0, \tau]$ (V9.17); $\lambda(1)$ is the index of $E_{**}$ on all of $T\Omega_\gamma$. (1) $\lambda(\tau) \le \lambda(\tau')$ for $\tau \le \tau'$. (2) $\lambda(\tau) = 0$ for $0 < \tau \le h_0$ (V9.16).

chips: restriction of $E_{**}$, not a new Hessian
diff: $\lambda(\tau)$ is the index of a restriction of $E_{**}$, not of a Hessian along $\gamma_\tau$ on its own interval: the fields along $\gamma_\tau$ vanishing at $0$ and $\tau$, extended by zero as in Milnor's proof of (1), with $\frac12E_{**}$ given on them by the integral over $[0, \tau]$ (V8.15). With this definition (1) is immediate, and no rescaling of $\gamma_\tau$ to $[0, 1]$ (the exposition's Lemma 13.B) is needed.

(2) comes from the Poincaré estimate (V9.16 (i)): $E_{**}$ is positive definite on the fields along $\gamma|[0, \tau]$ when $\tau \le h_0$. Milnor's route needs short geodesics to be minimal (Theorem 10.4) and Lemma 13.6.

items.title: The forms $H_\tau$ and their continuity (Lemma 15.C)

milnor.label: §15, p. 86
milnor.statement: With the subdivision chosen so that $t_i < \tau < t_{i+1}$, $\lambda(\tau)$ is the index of a quadratic form $H_\tau$ on the broken Jacobi fields along $\gamma_\tau$ for $0 < t_1 < \dots < t_i < \tau$, a space isomorphic to $\Sigma = TM_{\gamma(t_1)} \oplus \dots \oplus TM_{\gamma(t_i)}$, which is independent of $\tau$. "Evidently" $H_\tau$ varies continuously with $\tau$.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $\gamma$ be a smooth curve in $N$ on $[0, 1]$ and $B$ a finite set; $\tau$ is *valid* for $B$ if $0 < \tau \le 1$ and $B$ is fine for $[0, \tau]$. For valid $\tau$, $H_\tau$ is the symmetric bilinear form on $\Sigma = \bigoplus_{b \in B}T_{\gamma(b)}N$ given by $E_{**}$ on the broken Jacobi fields along $\gamma|[0, \tau]$ with these values at the points of $B$ (V9.17). For valid $\tau$, the index of $H_\tau$ is $\lambda(\tau)$ and its nullity is $\nu(\tau)$. For $x, y \in \Sigma$, $\tau \mapsto H_\tau(x, y)$ is continuous on the set of valid $\tau$; and if $B$ is fine for $[0, \tau]$ with its last point $m$ within $h_0/2$ of $\tau$, every $\tau' \in (m, \tau + h_0/2)$ with $\tau' \le 1$ is valid.

diff: The continuity needs that the subdivision stays fine for $\tau'$ near $\tau$, that the last division point and $\tau$ are not conjugate (so that the Jacobi field with prescribed values there exists), the linear dependence of Jacobi fields on their initial values, and the continuity of the solution of an injective linear system; all are supplied.

The formal proof reads $H_\tau$ through its jump terms (V9.18 (ii)), where only the covariant derivative at the last division point depends on $\tau$; this replaces Cramer's rule in the exposition's proof.

items.title: Assertion (3): $\lambda$ is continuous from the left

milnor.label: §15, Assertion (3)
milnor.statement: $\lambda(\tau - \varepsilon) = \lambda(\tau)$ for all sufficiently small $\varepsilon > 0$. Proof (p. 86): $H_\tau$ is negative definite on a subspace of $\Sigma$ of dimension $\lambda(\tau)$, hence so is $H_{\tau'}$ for $\tau'$ near $\tau$, giving $\lambda(\tau') \ge \lambda(\tau)$, and Assertion (1) gives the reverse inequality for $\tau' < \tau$.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: for a smooth curve $\gamma$ in $N$ on $[0, 1]$ and $0 < \tau \le 1$, $\lambda(\tau') = \lambda(\tau)$ for all $\tau' < \tau$ close enough to $\tau$, $\lambda$ as in V9.20.

diff: The proof is Milnor's, with V9.21 and the persistence of definiteness (V9.14 (3)); it needs $\lambda(\tau)$ finite and attained (V9.13, V9.19).

items.title: Theorem 15.1: the Morse index theorem

milnor.label: §15, Theorem 15.1
milnor.statement: (Morse.) The index $\lambda$ of $E_{**}$ is equal to the number of points $\gamma(t)$, with $0 < t < 1$, such that $\gamma(t)$ is conjugate to $\gamma(0)$ along $\gamma$, each such conjugate point being counted with its multiplicity. The index $\lambda$ is always finite. On p. 87 the theorem "clearly follows" from Assertions (2), (3) and (4).

chips: the identity along any smooth curve
finiteness of the set proved first
diff: Conjugate parameters replace conjugate points (V9.4), as Milnor's footnote of p. 77 recommends for geodesics with self-intersections.
(ii) holds along any smooth curve in $N$; when $\gamma$ is not a geodesic, $E_{**}$ is the form of V8.14, not the Hessian of the energy.

"Clearly follows" hides a step: the finiteness of the set of conjugate parameters has to be proved first, from Assertions (1) and (4) and the finiteness of $\lambda(1)$, before the jumps can be added up; then $\lambda(\tau) - \sum_{t < \tau}\nu(t)$ is locally constant on $(0, 1]$, and it vanishes for small $\tau$.

items.title: Corollary 15.2: finitely many conjugate points

milnor.label: §15, Corollary 15.2
milnor.statement: A geodesic segment $\gamma : [0, 1] \to M$ can contain only finitely many points which are conjugate to $\gamma(0)$ along $\gamma$; an "immediate consequence" of Theorem 15.1.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: for a geodesic $\gamma \in \Omega(N; p, q)$, the set of parameters conjugate to $0$ along $\gamma$ is finite.

diff: Conjugate parameters replace conjugate points (V9.4); the proof is V9.24, plus the parameter $t = 1$.

items.title: Milnor's metric on $\Omega$

milnor.label: §16, p. 88
milnor.statement: The path space $\Omega$ can be topologized by the distance $d(\omega, \omega') = \max_t\rho(\omega(t), \omega'(t)) + \big[\int_0^1(\frac{ds}{dt} - \frac{ds'}{dt})^2dt\big]^{1/2}$, where $s(t)$ and $s'(t)$ are the arc lengths of $\omega$ and $\omega'$ from $0$ to $t$, and $\rho$ is the distance of §10.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric and its distance $\rho$ (V7.18): for $\omega, \eta \in \Omega(N; p, q)$, with speeds $\dot s_\omega = \|\omega'\|$ and $\dot s_\eta = \|\eta'\|$, $$d(\omega, \eta) = \sup_{0 \le t \le 1}\rho(\omega(t), \eta(t)) + \Big(\int_0^1(\dot s_\omega - \dot s_\eta)^2\,dt\Big)^{1/2}.$$ This is an extended pseudometric on $\Omega$ (values in $[0, \infty]$, symmetric, with the triangle inequality), and two paths that agree on $[0, 1]$ are at distance $0$. From now on $\Omega$ and its subsets carry the topology of $d$.

chips: a pseudometric on maps $\mathbb R \to V$
diff: Paths are maps on $\mathbb R$ whose values off $[0, 1]$ play no role, and $d$ sees only $[0, 1]$, so it is a pseudometric; on paths $[0, 1] \to N$ it is Milnor's metric. Three conventions follow throughout the chapter: identities between paths hold on $[0, 1]$, homeomorphisms become homotopy equivalences up to paths at distance $0$, and geodesics are counted by their values on $[0, 1]$.
The triangle inequality for the second term is Minkowski's inequality in $L^2$; $\frac{ds}{dt}$ exists except at finitely many points.

items.title: The energy is continuous for $d$ (Lemmas 16.A and 16.B)

milnor.label: §16, p. 88
milnor.statement: The last term of $d$ is added so that the energy $E_a^b(\omega) = \int_a^b(\frac{ds}{dt})^2dt$ is a continuous function on $\Omega$. Hence $\Omega^c = E^{-1}([0, c])$ is closed and $\operatorname{Int}\Omega^c = E^{-1}([0, c))$ is open.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: (i) for $\omega, \eta \in \Omega$ and $0 \le a \le b \le 1$, $|\sqrt{E_a^b(\omega)} - \sqrt{E_a^b(\eta)}| \le (\int_0^1(\dot s_\omega - \dot s_\eta)^2dt)^{1/2}$; hence $\sqrt{E_a^b}$ is $1$-Lipschitz for $d$, $E_a^b$ is continuous on $\Omega$, $\Omega^c$ is closed and $\operatorname{Int}\Omega^c$ is open. (ii) (Lemma 16.B) If $\omega_n \to \omega$ in $\Omega$, then for every $\epsilon > 0$ there is $\delta > 0$ with $E_a^b(\omega_n) < \epsilon$ for all $n$ and all $0 \le a \le b \le 1$ with $b - a < \delta$.

chips: uniformly small energy on short intervals
diff: $\sqrt{E_a^b} = \|\dot s\|_{L^2[a, b]}$, and Minkowski's inequality on $[a, b]$ makes it $1$-Lipschitz for $d$; with the uniform term alone the energy is not continuous.
(ii) is not in the book; it is what the continuity of Milnor's deformation $r_u$ needs (V10.7). The Lipschitz bound is also what makes Milnor's map $h$ of §17 discontinuous (V10.19′).

items.title: The ball $S$, subdivisions, and Milnor’s choices

milnor.label: §16, pp. 88–89
milnor.statement: $\Omega(t_0, \dots, t_k)$ is the space of paths $\omega$ with each $\omega|[t_{i-1}, t_i]$ a geodesic, and $\operatorname{Int}\Omega(t_0, \dots, t_k)^c = (\operatorname{Int}\Omega^c) \cap \Omega(t_0, \dots, t_k)$ (p. 88). On p. 89: every $\omega \in \Omega^c$ lies in the ball $S$ of radius $\sqrt c$ about $p$, by $L^2 \le E \le c$; $S$ is compact since $M$ is complete; by 10.8 there is $\varepsilon > 0$ such that two points of $S$ at distance less than $\varepsilon$ are joined by a unique geodesic of length less than $\varepsilon$, depending differentiably on them; and the subdivision is chosen with each $t_i - t_{i-1} < \varepsilon^2/c$.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $c > 0$ and $S = \{x \in N : \rho(p, x) \le \sqrt c\}$. (i) Every $\omega \in \Omega$ with $E(\omega) \le c$ maps $[0, 1]$ into $S$. (ii) $S$ is compact if $N$ is closed in $V$, or connected and complete. (iii) For every compact $K \subseteq N$ there is $\delta > 0$ such that points of $K$ at distance $< \delta$ are joined as in Corollary 10.8 at the scale $\delta$, and $\delta$ is at most a normal radius at every point of $K$. (iv) *Milnor's data* (V10.3): $p, q \in N$, $c > 0$ with $S = \{x \in N : \rho(p, x) \le \sqrt c\}$ compact, a scale $\delta$ as in Corollary 10.8 for $K = S$ that is also at most a normal radius on $S$ (Milnor's $\varepsilon$), and a subdivision $0 = t_0 < \dots < t_{m+1} = 1$ with $c\,(t_{i+1} - t_i) < \delta^2$. If $p, q \in N$ and $S$ is compact, every subdivision of small enough mesh, and some subdivision into equal parts, is part of such data. (v) For Milnor's data, $B = \operatorname{Int}\Omega(t_0, \dots, t_k)^c$ is the set of $\omega \in \Omega$ with $E(\omega) < c$ that are geodesics on each $(t_i, t_{i+1})$, and $B^a = \{\omega \in B : E(\omega) \le a\}$.

diff: Completeness enters only as the compactness of $S$, which is the Hopf–Rinow theorem (Corollary 10.10, V7.27) and holds in particular when $N$ is closed in $V$.
$\delta$ is also asked to be at most a normal radius on $S$, which (iii) provides at no cost and which keeps the ends of each segment non-conjugate (V10.10).

items.title: Lemma 16.1: the manifold of broken geodesics

milnor.label: §16, Lemma 16.1
milnor.statement: Let $M$ be complete and $c > 0$ with $\Omega^c$ non-vacuous. Then for all sufficiently fine subdivisions $(t_0, \dots, t_k)$ of $[0, 1]$, $\operatorname{Int}\Omega(t_0, \dots, t_k)^c$ can be given the structure of a smooth finite dimensional manifold "in a natural way". Proof (p. 89): for a broken geodesic $(L_{t_{i-1}}^{t_i}\omega)^2 = (t_i - t_{i-1})E_{t_{i-1}}^{t_i}\omega < \varepsilon^2$, so each segment is determined by its end points, and $\omega$ by $(\omega(t_1), \dots, \omega(t_{k-1})) \in M \times \dots \times M$; this is a homeomorphism onto an open subset of the product, whose differentiable structure is taken over.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: fix Milnor's data. For $y = (y_1, \dots, y_m) \in V^m$ put $x_0 = p$, $x_j = y_j$, $x_{m+1} = q$, and $E'(y) = \sum_{i=0}^m\rho(x_i, x_{i+1})^2/(t_{i+1} - t_i)$; let $U$ be the set of $y \in N^m$ with every $\rho(x_i, x_{i+1})$ finite and $E'(y) < c$. (i) $U = N^m \cap O$ for an open $O \subseteq V^m$, and every such set is a slice submanifold of $V^m$, with tangent space $T_{y_1}N \times \dots \times T_{y_m}N$. (ii) For $y \in U$, the broken geodesic $\omega_y$, on $[t_i, t_{i+1}]$ the short geodesic from $x_i$ to $x_{i+1}$ run at constant speed, lies in $B$, has break points $y$, and $E(\omega_y) = E'(y)$. (iii) Every $\omega \in B$ has its break points $y$ in $U$, and $\omega_y = \omega$ on $[0, 1]$. So $y \mapsto \omega_y$ and $\omega \mapsto (\omega(t_1), \dots, \omega(t_m))$ are inverse bijections between $U$ and $B$, paths compared on $[0, 1]$.

diff: Milnor's hypothesis that $\Omega^c$ is non-vacuous is not needed (an empty manifold is a manifold).
The manifold is the open subset $U$ of $N^m$, rather than a structure transported to $B$; the topologies are compared in V10.5.

Hidden: that the image is exactly the open set $U$ (the vertices of a point of $U$ lie in $S$ by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, consecutive ones at distance $< \delta$); that a geodesic segment is the radial geodesic of its initial vector (V9.9) and, that vector being shorter than $\delta$, the short geodesic; and that a broken geodesic is smooth up to the ends of its segments.

items.title: Broken geodesics and their break points: a homeomorphism up to distance $0$

milnor.label: §16, p. 89
milnor.statement: "Evidently" the correspondence $\omega \mapsto (\omega(t_1), \dots, \omega(t_{k-1}))$ defines a homeomorphism between $\operatorname{Int}\Omega(t_0, \dots, t_k)^c$ and an open subset of $M \times \dots \times M$.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: for Milnor's data, $y \mapsto \omega_y$ is continuous from $U$ (topology of $V^m$) to $(\Omega, d)$, and $\omega \mapsto (\omega(t_1), \dots, \omega(t_m))$ is continuous from $\Omega$ to $V^m$. For every $a$ they restrict to continuous maps between $B^a$ and $\{y \in U : E'(y) \le a\}$, inverse to each other up to paths at distance $0$; so the two sets are homotopy equivalent (for $a \ge c$, $B$ and $U$).

diff: A homotopy equivalence, indeed a homeomorphism up to the identification of paths at distance $0$, replaces the homeomorphism, since paths are maps on $\mathbb R$.

"Evidently" hides the continuity of $y \mapsto \omega_y$ for $d$: the uniform term needs the continuity of short geodesics in their end points (Corollary 10.8 and the continuity of $\exp$, V7.23), and the $L^2$ term that of the speeds $\rho(x_i, x_{i+1})/(t_{i+1} - t_i)$.

items.title: Theorem 16.2: $E'$ is smooth and $B^a$ is compact

milnor.label: §16, Theorem 16.2, pp. 90–91
milnor.statement: The function $E' : B \to \mathbb R$, the restriction of $E$, is smooth; for each $a < c$ the set $B^a = (E')^{-1}[0, a]$ is compact. On p. 90 $E'$ depends smoothly on the break points by the explicit formula $E'(\omega) = \sum_i\rho(\omega(t_{i-1}), \omega(t_i))^2/(t_i - t_{i-1})$; on p. 91 $B^a$ is homeomorphic to a set of $(k - 1)$-tuples in $S \times \dots \times S$ that is closed in a compact set.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: for Milnor's data: (i) every $y_0 \in U$ has an open neighbourhood $O$ in $V^m$ with a function smooth on $O$ that equals $E'$ on $U \cap O$; hence $E'$ is continuous on $U$, and smooth on the manifold $N^m \cap O$ for every open $O \subseteq V^m$ with $N^m \cap O \subseteq U$. (ii) For $a < c$, $\{y \in U : E'(y) \le a\}$ is compact.

diff: $\rho$ is not smooth on the diagonal; $E'$ is smooth because $\rho(x, x')^2 = \|v(x, x')\|^2$ with $v$ the smooth initial vector of Corollary 10.8. The set of tuples is closed only because the distances are finite.

As reproduced in the scan, the condition defining the tuples reads $\rho(p_{i-1}, p_i)^c/(t_i - t_{i-1}) \le a$, with exponent $c$ and no summation sign; the formal condition is $E'(p_1, \dots, p_{k-1}) \le a$, the sum with exponent $2$.
Compactness is stated for the set of break points, which is homotopy equivalent to $B^a$ by V10.5.

items.title: Milnor’s deformation $r_u$ (Lemma 16.C)

milnor.label: §16, p. 91
milnor.statement: The retraction $r : \operatorname{Int}\Omega^c \to B$ sends $\omega$ to the broken geodesic which on each $[t_{i-1}, t_i]$ is the geodesic of length less than $\varepsilon$ from $\omega(t_{i-1})$ to $\omega(t_i)$; "clearly" $E(r(\omega)) \le E(\omega) < c$. For $t_{i-1} \le u \le t_i$, $r_u(\omega)$ is $r(\omega)$ on $[0, t_{i-1}]$, the minimal geodesic from $\omega(t_{i-1})$ to $\omega(u)$ on $[t_{i-1}, u]$, and $\omega$ on $[u, 1]$; $r_0$ is the identity, $r_1 = r$, and "it is easily verified" that $r_u(\omega)$ is continuous as a function of both variables.

lean.statement: For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: for Milnor's data, $\omega \in \Omega$ with $E(\omega) < c$ and $t_i \le u \le t_{i+1}$, $r_u(\omega)$ is the broken geodesic of the break points of $\omega$ on $[0, t_i]$, the short geodesic from $\omega(t_i)$ to $\omega(u)$ at constant speed on $[t_i, u]$, and $\omega$ on $[u, 1]$; the formulas of neighbouring segments agree at $u = t_{i+1}$. On $[0, 1]$: $r_u(\omega) \in \Omega$, $E(r_u(\omega)) \le E(\omega)$, $r_0(\omega) = \omega$, $r_1(\omega) = \omega_y$ for the break points $y$ of $\omega$, and $r_u(\omega) = \omega$ for $\omega \in B$. Completed by $\omega$ off $[0, 1]$, and by $\omega$ itself when $u \notin [0, 1]$ or $E(\omega) \ge c$, $(u, \omega) \mapsto r_u(\omega)$ is a map $\mathbb R \times \Omega \to \Omega$, continuous on $[0, 1] \times \operatorname{Int}\Omega^c$.

diff: Milnor's minimal geodesic is the short geodesic of Corollary 10.8, which is minimal; it exists since $\rho(\omega(t_i), \omega(u))^2 \le (u - t_i)E(\omega) < \delta^2$.

Hidden: the formulas must agree where neighbouring intervals meet; $r_u$ fixes $B$ because a sub-arc of a short geodesic is the short geodesic between its ends; and $E(r_u(\omega)) \le E(\omega)$ holds segment by segment, by $\rho^2 \le (b - a)E_a^b$.

The continuity needs, for the uniform term, the continuity of short geodesics in their end points and the equicontinuity of the paths of energy $< c$, and, for the $L^2$ term near $u = t_i$, the bound $\rho(\omega(t_i), \omega(u))^2/(u - t_i) \le E_{t_i}^u(\omega)$ with Lemma 16.B (V10.2).

items.title: Theorem 16.2: $B^a$ is a deformation retract of $\Omega^a$

milnor.label: §16, Theorem 16.2, pp. 90–91
milnor.statement: For each $a < c$, $B^a$ is a deformation retract of $\Omega^a$; a footnote adds that $B$ itself is similarly a deformation retract of $\operatorname{Int}\Omega^c$. On p. 91: since $E(r_u(\omega)) \le E(\omega)$, "it is clear" that each $B^a$ is a deformation retract of $\Omega^a$.
