The description of $\Omega_k(n)$ near $J$ as the points $J\exp A$, $A$ in a linear subspace, "clearly implies" that $\Omega_k(n)$ is a totally geodesic submanifold of $O(n)$.

lean.statement: Let $N \subseteq M_n(\mathbb R)$ be a slice submanifold consisting of orthogonal matrices, and for each $x \in N$ let $T_x$ be a space of skew matrices with $\dim T_x = \dim N$, such that $x\exp A \in N$ and $A \in T_{x\exp A}$ whenever $A \in T_x$. Then: (i) the tangent space of $N$ at $x$ is $x\,T_x$; (ii) for $A \in T_x$ the curve $t \mapsto x\exp(tA)$ is a geodesic of $N$ on all of $\mathbb R$; (iii) every unbroken geodesic $\gamma \in \Omega(N; p, q)$ agrees on $[0, 1]$ with $s \mapsto p\exp(sV)$ for some $V \in T_p$; (iv) the Riemannian exponential of $N$ is $\exp_x(xA) = x\exp A$ for $A \in T_x$, and $N$ is geodesically complete. Also, as a tool for V15.23: let $S$ be a subset of a real normed space $V$ such that near each $x \in S$ there is a smooth $\Phi : Z \times W \to V$ ($Z$, $W$ finite-dimensional) with $\Phi(0) = x$ and invertible derivative at $0$, for which, near $0$, the points $\Phi(z, 0)$ lie in $S$ and every point $\Phi(q) \in S$ equals $\Phi(g(q), 0)$ with $g(q) \to 0$ as $q \to 0$; then $S$ is a slice submanifold modelled on $Z$.

diff: What Milnor uses of "totally geodesic" is the list of geodesics: they are the curves $x\exp(tA)$, $A \in T_x$. This is proved from the normality of the acceleration $x\exp(tA)A^2$, without comparing the geodesics of $N$ with those of $O(n)$.
The exponential map of $N$ is $xA \mapsto x\exp A$, so $N$ is complete.

items.title: Assertions 1 and 2 in both directions; $\Omega_k(n)$ near a point

milnor.label: §24, Assertions 1 and 2, p. 137
milnor.statement: For small skew $A$: $J\exp A$ is a complex structure if and only if $A$ anticommutes with $J$; $J\exp A$ anticommutes with $J_1, \dots, J_{k-1}$ if and only if $A$ commutes with them. Thus a neighborhood of $J$ in $\Omega_k(n)$ consists of all points $J\exp A$ where $A$ ranges over all small matrices in a linear subspace of the Lie algebra.

lean.statement: For a matrix $x$ let $\mathcal T_x$ be the space of skew matrices $A$ with $Ax = -xA$ and $AJ_\alpha = J_\alpha A$ for $1 \le \alpha \le k - 1$; for $k = 0$ the first condition is dropped, so that $\mathcal T_x$ is the space $\mathfrak o(n)$ of all skew matrices, the same for every $x$. (i) For any fixed matrices $J_\alpha$: if $x \in \Omega_k(n)$ and $A \in \mathcal T_x$, then $x\exp A \in \Omega_k(n)$ and $A \in \mathcal T_{x\exp A}$. (ii) There is $\varepsilon > 0$ such that $\exp$ is injective on the matrices of norm $< \varepsilon$. For every such $\varepsilon$, every anticommuting family $J_1, \dots, J_k$, every $x \in \Omega_k(n)$ and every matrix $C$ with $\|C\| < \varepsilon$: if $x\exp C \in \Omega_k(n)$, then $C \in \mathcal T_x$. (iii) Hence, for an anticommuting family and $x \in \Omega_k(n)$, there is a map $L$ with $L(y) \to 0$ as $y \to x$, such that every $y \in \Omega_k(n)$ near $x$ satisfies $L(y) \in \mathcal T_x$ and $y = x\exp(L(y))$.

diff: "Since $A$ is small" is the injectivity of $\exp$ on a ball, applied to $C^{\mathsf T}$, $x^{\mathsf T}Cx$ and $J_\alpha CJ_\alpha^{\mathsf T}$; the ball must be invariant under transposition and orthogonal conjugation, as the Frobenius ball is.
In the converse $C$ is any small matrix with $x\exp C \in \Omega_k(n)$; that it is skew is a conclusion.

items.title: Lemma 24.4, first half: a smooth, totally geodesic submanifold

milnor.label: §24, Lemma 24.4
milnor.statement: Each $\Omega_k(n)$ is a smooth, totally geodesic submanifold of $O(n)$.
milnor.note: p. 139: $\Omega_3(16r)$ "contains components of varying dimension"; p. 141: so does $\Omega_7(16r)$.

lean.statement: The *stratum* of $\Omega_k(n)$ through a matrix $p$ is the set of $x \in \Omega_k(n)$ with $\dim\mathcal T_x = \dim\mathcal T_p$. (i) $\dim\mathcal T_{x\exp A} = \dim\mathcal T_x$ for $A \in \mathcal T_x$. Let $J_1, \dots, J_k$ be an anticommuting family. (ii) The stratum is open in $\Omega_k(n)$ (each of its points has a neighbourhood in $M_n(\mathbb R)$ whose points in $\Omega_k(n)$ belong to it), closed in $M_n(\mathbb R)$, and compact. (iii) It is a slice submanifold of $M_n(\mathbb R)$ modelled on $\mathcal T_p$, and it satisfies the hypotheses of V15.21 with $T_x = \mathcal T_x$. Consequently its tangent space at $x$ is $x\mathcal T_x$, its geodesics are the curves $t \mapsto x\exp(tA)$ with $A \in \mathcal T_x$, and it is geodesically complete. For $k = 0$ the stratum through any $p$ is $O(n)$.

diff: $\Omega_k(n)$ is not a manifold of one dimension. The statement is for the stratum through $p$, the set where $\dim\mathcal T_x = \dim\mathcal T_p$, which is open and closed in $\Omega_k(n)$ and compact.
It is a submanifold of the space of matrices, with tangent spaces $x\mathcal T_x$ and geodesics $x\exp(tA)$, $A \in \mathcal T_x$ (V15.21).

items.title: Lemma 24.1: the length of a geodesic from $I$ to $-I$

milnor.label: §24, proof of Lemma 24.1, p. 134
milnor.statement: In the block normal form with $a_1, \dots, a_m \ge 0$: $\exp(\pi A) = -I$ if and only if $a_1, \dots, a_m$ are odd integers; $\langle A, A\rangle = 2(a_1^2 + \dots + a_m^2)$; therefore the geodesic $\exp(\pi tA)$ from $I$ to $-I$ is minimal if and only if $a_1 = \dots = a_m = 1$, and then $A^2 = -I$.

lean.statement: Let $V$ be a skew matrix with $\exp V = -I$. If $E \neq 0$ is a matrix and $V^2E = -\lambda E$ for a real $\lambda$, then $\lambda \ge \pi^2$. Hence $\|V\|^2 \ge \pi^2n$, and if $\|V\|^2 \le \pi^2n$ then $V^2 = -\pi^2I$.

diff: For skew $V$ with $\exp V = -I$, every eigenvalue of $V^{\mathsf T}V$ is $\ge \pi^2$; so $\|V\|^2 \ge \pi^2n$, with equality only if $V^2 = -\pi^2I$. Proved by the spectral theorem and an argument with $c' = Vc$ for each eigenvalue, not by the normal form.

items.title: The distance from $J_k$ to $-J_k$, and the minimal geodesics

milnor.label: §24, proof of Lemma 24.4, pp. 137–138
milnor.statement: $t \mapsto J_k\exp(\pi tA)$ defines a geodesic from $J_k$ to $-J_k$ in $\Omega_k(n)$; "since this geodesic is minimal in $O(n)$, it is certainly minimal in $\Omega_k(n)$". Conversely, a minimal geodesic from $J_k$ to $-J_k$ in $\Omega_k(n)$ is $J_k\exp(\pi tA)$ with $A$ a complex structure (by 24.1) which commutes with $J_1, \dots, J_{k-1}$ and anticommutes with $J_k$. Remark: $J_kA$ is the midpoint $\gamma(\tfrac12)$.

lean.statement: Let $J_1, \dots, J_k$ be an anticommuting family, $p \in \Omega_k(n)$, $N$ the stratum through $p$, and $\mathcal C_p = \{A \in \mathcal T_p : A^2 = -I\}$; suppose $\mathcal C_p \neq \emptyset$. For $A \in \mathcal C_p$ put $\gamma_A(t) = p\exp(\pi tA)$. Then: (i) $-p \in N$; (ii) the Riemannian distance in $N$ is $\rho(p, -p) = \pi\sqrt n$, and every path in $\Omega(N; p, -p)$ has energy $\ge \pi^2n$; (iii) every $\gamma_A$, $A \in \mathcal C_p$, is a path of least energy in $\Omega(N; p, -p)$, and its midpoint is $\gamma_A(\tfrac12) = pA$; (iv) every path of least energy agrees on $[0, 1]$ with $\gamma_A$ for some $A \in \mathcal C_p$.

diff: Distances in $\Omega_k(n)$ and in $O(n)$ are not compared: the stratum is complete, so a shortest geodesic exists (Hopf–Rinow, V7.26); it is $p\exp(tV)$ with $\exp V = -I$, and $\|V\| \ge \pi\sqrt n$ (V15.24).
"Minimal" is "of least energy". The statement holds at every $p \in \Omega_k(n)$ for which some $A \in \mathcal T_p$ has $A^2 = -I$.

items.title: Lemma 24.1, and Lemma 24.4, second half: minimal geodesics and $\Omega_{k+1}(n)$

milnor.label: §24, Lemma 24.1, p. 133; Lemma 24.4, p. 136
milnor.statement: The space of minimal geodesics from $I$ to $-I$ in $O(n)$ is homeomorphic to the space $\Omega_1(n)$ of complex structures on $\mathbb R^n$ (24.1). The space of minimal geodesics from $J_\ell$ to $-J_\ell$ in $\Omega_\ell(n)$ is homeomorphic to $\Omega_{\ell+1}(n)$, for $0 \le \ell < k$ (24.4).

lean.statement: Let $J_1, \dots, J_k$ be an anticommuting family, with base point $J_k$ ($J_0 = I$). (i) $A \in \mathcal C_{J_k}$ if and only if $J_kA \in \Omega_{k+1}(n)$; $A \mapsto J_kA$ is a homeomorphism of $\mathcal C_{J_k}$ onto $\Omega_{k+1}(n)$, with inverse $J' \mapsto J_k^{\mathsf T}J'$; and for $J' \in \Omega_{k+1}(n)$ and $A = J_k^{\mathsf T}J'$, $\gamma_A(t) = \cos(\pi t)\,J_k + \sin(\pi t)\,J'$ for all $t$. (ii) In the setting of V15.25, $A \mapsto \gamma_A$ is a homotopy equivalence of $\mathcal C_p$ with $\Omega^d(N; p, -p)$, and a homeomorphism of $\mathcal C_p$ onto the quotient of $\Omega^d$ in which paths at distance $0$ are identified. (iii) If $J_1, \dots, J_{k+1}$ is an anticommuting family and $N$ is the stratum of $\Omega_k(n)$ through $J_k$, the map $\varphi : \Omega_{k+1}(n) \to \Omega(N; J_k, -J_k)$, $\varphi(J')(t) = \cos(\pi t)\,J_k + \sin(\pi t)\,J'$, is continuous, and it is the inclusion $\Omega^d \to \Omega$ composed with a homotopy equivalence $\Omega_{k+1}(n) \to \Omega^d$. For $k = 0$, $N = O(n)$ and $\Omega_1(n)$ is the set of all complex structures: this is Lemma 24.1.

chips: a homotopy equivalence on the nose
diff: The minimal directions $A$ correspond homeomorphically to the points $J' = J_kA$ of $\Omega_{k+1}(n)$, and the geodesic of $J'$ is the semicircle $\cos(\pi t)J_k + \sin(\pi t)J'$.

Paths are functions on $\mathbb R$, so the space $\Omega^d$ of minimal paths is homotopy equivalent to $\Omega_{k+1}(n)$, and homeomorphic to it only after identifying paths that agree on $[0, 1]$. Milnor's "$0 \le \ell < k$" tacitly needs $\Omega_{\ell+1}(n) \neq \emptyset$.

items.title: The neighbourhood retraction for $\Omega_k(n)$

milnor.label: §24, pp. 135–136
milnor.statement: Theorem 22.1 is applied with "the statement that $\Omega_1(n)$ is a manifold" (and likewise for $\Omega_{k+1}(n)$). No retraction is written down.

lean.statement: In the setting of V15.25, $\Omega^d(N; p, -p)$ is a retract of an open neighbourhood: there are an open $O \supseteq \Omega^d$ in $\Omega(N; p, -p)$ and a map $\rho : O \to \Omega^d$, continuous on $O$ and equal to the identity on $\Omega^d$. Here, for a matrix $Y$, let $Y_1$ be the orthogonal projection of $p^{\mathsf T}Y$ onto $\mathcal T_p$; if $\det(Y_1^{\mathsf T}Y_1) \neq 0$, then $Y_1(Y_1^{\mathsf T}Y_1)^{-1/2} \in \mathcal C_p$. $O$ is the set of paths $\omega$ whose midpoint $Y = \omega(\tfrac12)$ has $\det(Y_1^{\mathsf T}Y_1) \neq 0$, an open set, and off $\Omega^d$ the retraction is $\rho(\omega) = \gamma_A$ with $A = Y_1(Y_1^{\mathsf T}Y_1)^{-1/2}$.

diff: This proves the hypothesis of V13.2 for every stratum: project $p^{\mathsf T}\omega(\tfrac12)$ onto $\mathcal T_p$ and take the polar part, the nearest complex structure in $\mathcal T_p$.

items.title: Killing fields are Jacobi fields; a lower bound for the index

milnor.label: §24, pp. 144, 146
milnor.statement: Since $\Omega_k(n)$ is a totally geodesic submanifold of $O(n)$, $K_A$ can be computed by $K_AB = -\tfrac14[A, [A, B]]$ on $T$. Each eigenvalue $e^2$ of $K_A$ gives rise to conjugate points for $t = e^{-1}, 2e^{-1}, 3e^{-1}, \dots$ by 20.5; then apply the index theorem.

lean.statement: Let $J_1, \dots, J_k$ be an anticommuting family, $p \in \Omega_k(n)$, $N$ the stratum through $p$, and $V \in \mathcal T_p$. The *isotropy algebra* of $p$ is the space of skew matrices commuting with $p$ and with $J_1, \dots, J_{k-1}$. (i) For $X$ in the isotropy algebra, $K(t) = X\gamma(t) - \gamma(t)X$ is a Jacobi field along $\gamma(t) = p\exp(tV)$ in $N$. (ii) Let $\gamma \in \Omega(N; p, q)$ be an unbroken geodesic equal to $t \mapsto p\exp(tV)$ on $[0, 1]$, let $\tau \in [0, 1]$, and let $\mathcal X$ be a subspace of the isotropy algebra whose elements commute with $\exp(\tau V)$ and none of whose non-zero elements commutes with $V$. Then $\gamma(\tau)$ is conjugate to $\gamma(0)$ along $\gamma$ with multiplicity (V9.4) at least $\dim\mathcal X$. (iii) For a finite set $T \subset (0, 1)$ and such subspaces $\mathcal X_\tau$, $\tau \in T$, the index of $\gamma$ is at least $\sum_{\tau \in T}\dim\mathcal X_\tau$.

diff: Neither the curvature of the totally geodesic $\Omega_k(n)$ nor Theorem 20.5 for it is formalized. For a lower bound, Jacobi fields vanishing at $0$ and $\tau$ suffice; they are the variation fields of the isometries $y \mapsto gyg^{-1}$, $g = \exp(uX)$, for $X$ commuting with $\exp(\tau V)$.
The index bound is then the Index Theorem (V9.24).

items.title: The splitting into minimal pieces; Lemma 24.8 between two pieces

milnor.label: §24, pp. 144–145
milnor.statement: $\mathbb R^n = M_1 \oplus \dots \oplus M_s$, mutually orthogonal subspaces closed and minimal under the action of $J_1, \dots, J_{k-1}$, $J$ and $A$. The eigenvalues of $A$ on $M_h$ "must be all equal, except for sign": $\pm ia_h$, with $a_h$ odd and positive. $J' = a_h^{-1}JA|M_h$ makes $M_h$ a minimal $(J_1, \dots, J_{k-1}, J, J')$-space, so $\dim M_h = m_{k+1}$ and $s = n/m_{k+1}$. For $h \neq j$ an isometry from $M_h$ to $\bar M_j$ "exists by 24.8".

lean.statement: Let $E$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and $\mathcal G$ a set of operators on $E$, each self-adjoint or skew-adjoint. A subspace is *minimal invariant* if it is non-zero, invariant under $\mathcal G$, and contains no invariant subspace other than $0$ and itself. (i) Every invariant subspace $U$ is spanned by a list of pairwise orthogonal minimal invariant subspaces of $U$ whose dimensions add up to $\dim U$; and a self-adjoint operator that commutes with $\mathcal G$ and preserves a minimal invariant $M$ is a scalar on $M$. (ii) Let $A$ be skew-adjoint, let $J, J_1, \dots, J_{k-1}$ be skew-adjoint operators with square $-1$, anticommuting with one another, and let $A$ anticommute with $J$ and commute with the $J_\alpha$ (for $k = 0$: $J = 1$ and there are no $J_\alpha$); put $\mathcal G = \{A, J, J_1, \dots, J_{k-1}\}$. On each minimal invariant $M$, $A^2 = -c$ for a real $c$; and for real $s$ with $s^2c = 1$ the restrictions of $J_1, \dots, J_{k-1}, J, sJA$ to $M$ satisfy the Clifford relations (V15.10) and make $M$ a minimal space for $k + 1$ structures (V15.13). For matrices: if $A$ is skew, $\exp(\pi A) = -I$, and $A^2 = -c$ on a non-zero subspace of $\mathbb R^n$, then $c \ge 1$. (iii) If $k \le 7$, $k \not\equiv 2 \pmod 4$, and $M_0$, $M_1$ are minimal invariant with $A^2 = -a_0^2$ on $M_0$ and $A^2 = -b^2$ on $M_1$, $a_0, b > 0$, there is a linear isomorphism $T : M_0 \to M_1$ that commutes with $J$ and the $J_\alpha$ and carries $a_0^{-1}JA$ to $-b^{-1}JA$. (iv) If moreover $c \ge 1$ on every minimal invariant subspace and $A^2 \neq -1$, then in a splitting (i) of $E$ some piece $M_0$ has $c > 1$; and there are an integer $s$ with $(s + 1)m_{k+1} = \dim E$, reals $a_0 > 1$ and $b_1, \dots, b_s \ge 1$, and operators $D_1, \dots, D_s$ on $E$ (each the projection onto $M_0$ followed by an isomorphism (iii) onto another piece) which commute with $J$ and the $J_\alpha$, satisfy $b_jD_jA = -a_0AD_j$, $A^2D_j = -b_j^2D_j$ and $D_jA^2 = -a_0^2D_j$, and for which the $AD_j$ are separated by projections (for $k = 0$ there are two for each $j$, $D_j$ and $D_jA$).

diff: $a_h = \sqrt c$, where $A^2 = -c$ on the piece; that $a_h$ is an odd integer is not used, only $c \ge 1$. Complements of invariant subspaces are invariant because the operators are skew.
Milnor changes the sign of $J$ on $M_j$; changing the sign of the last structure instead is equivalent and keeps $T$ commuting with $J$. $T$ is linear, not isometric, which suffices.

items.title: Lemma 24.2, and the index of a non-minimal geodesic for $k \not\equiv 2 \pmod 4$

milnor.label: §24, Lemma 24.2, p. 135; Assertion, p. 146
milnor.statement: Any non-minimal geodesic from $I$ to $-I$ in $O(2m)$ has index $\ge 2m - 2$ (Lemma 24.2). For $k \not\equiv 2 \pmod 4$, the index of a non-minimal geodesic from $J$ to $-J$ in $\Omega_k(n)$ is $\ge n/m_{k+1} - 1$ (Assertion).

lean.statement:
Let $J_1, \dots, J_k$ be an anticommuting family on $\mathbb R^n$ with $\mathcal C_{J_k} 
eq \emptyset$ (equivalently $\Omega_{k+1}(n) 
eq \emptyset$, V15.26), let $k \le 7$ and $k 
ot\equiv 2 \pmod 4$, and let $N$ be the stratum through $J_k$. If $\gamma \in \Omega(N; J_k, -J_k)$ is an unbroken geodesic which is not of least energy, then $m_{k+1}$ divides $n$ and the index of $\gamma$ is at least $n/m_{k+1} - 1$; for $k = 0$ it is at least $2(n/2 - 1) = n - 2$.

diff: For $k = 0$ this is Lemma 24.2 as stated; for $1 \le k \le 7$, Milnor's Assertion. The Jacobi fields come from $X_j = D_j - D_j^{\mathsf T}$, with $D_j$ the intertwiners of V15.29, which commute with $\exp(\tau_j\pi A)$ at $\tau_j = 2/(a_0 + b_j)$; their independence, which Milnor does not discuss, is proved.
The exact formula of Lemma 24.2 is not proved for geodesics (V15.3). "Non-minimal" is "not of least energy".

items.title: Theorem 24.5 for each $n$, $k \not\equiv 2 \pmod 4$

milnor.label: §24, p. 146; Theorem 24.5, p. 138
milnor.statement: The inclusion map $\Omega_{k+1}(n) \to \Omega\Omega_k(n)$ induces isomorphisms of homotopy groups in dimensions $\le n/m_{k+1} - 3$. (Theorem 24.5: $\pi_hO \cong \pi_{h-1}\Omega_1 \cong \pi_{h-2}\Omega_2 \cong \dots \cong \pi_1\Omega_{h-1}$.)

lean.statement: Let $J_1, \dots, J_{k+1}$ be an anticommuting family on $\mathbb R^n$, $k \le 7$, $k \not\equiv 2 \pmod 4$, let $N$ be the stratum of $\Omega_k(n)$ through $J_k$, and let $i + 2 \le n/m_{k+1} - 1$ (for $k = 0$: $i + 2 \le n - 2$). Then: (i) the inclusion $\Omega^d \to \Omega(N; J_k, -J_k)$ induces a bijection on $\pi_i$ at every minimal path; (ii) for every $J' \in \Omega_{k+1}(n)$, the map $\varphi$ of V15.26 induces a bijection $\pi_i(\Omega_{k+1}(n), J') \to \pi_i(\Omega(N; J_k, -J_k), \varphi(J'))$; (iii) for every $J' \in \Omega_{k+1}(n)$ there is a bijection $\pi_i(\Omega_{k+1}(n), J') \cong \pi_{i+1}(\Omega_k(n), J_k)$. On the way: $N$ is open and closed in $\Omega_k(n)$, and $\pi_{j+1}(N, x) \cong \pi_{j+1}(\Omega_k(n), x)$ for $x \in N$ and $j \ge 0$.

diff: Theorem 22.1 and Corollary 22.2 (V13.2–V13.4) for the stratum of $J_k$, with the retraction of V15.27 and the index bound of V15.30. The path space is that of piecewise smooth paths with Milnor's metric.
Also $\pi_i\Omega_{k+1}(n) \cong \pi_{i+1}\Omega_k(n)$, as sets; the stratum is open and closed in $\Omega_k(n)$ and carries its higher homotopy groups.

items.title: Theorem 24.3 (Bott)

milnor.label: §24, Theorem 24.3
milnor.statement: The inclusion map $\Omega_1(n) \to \Omega O(n)$ induces isomorphisms of homotopy groups in dimensions $\le n - 4$. Hence $\pi_i\Omega_1(n) \cong \pi_{i+1}O(n)$ for $i \le n - 4$.

lean.statement: Suppose $\mathbb R^n$ carries a complex structure (so $n$ is even), and let $i + 4 \le n$. For every complex structure $J'$ on $\mathbb R^n$, the map $\varphi : \Omega_1(n) \to \Omega(O(n); I, -I)$, $\varphi(J)(t) = \cos(\pi t)\,I + \sin(\pi t)\,J$, induces a bijection on $\pi_i$ at $J'$, and there is a bijection $\pi_i(\Omega_1(n), J') \cong \pi_{i+1}(O(n), I)$.

diff: The case $k = 0$ of V15.31: the stratum is $O(n)$ itself, and the range is $i + 2 \le n - 2$. The second isomorphism is a bijection of sets, not shown to be a homomorphism.

items.title: Angles, and the paths with a given end angle

milnor.label: §24, pp. 147–148
milnor.statement: $f$ maps the geodesic into a closed loop on $S^1$ "which is completely determined by the trace of $A$. It follows that this trace is invariant under homotopy of the geodesic within the path space". Then: "restrict attention to some fixed component of $\Omega\Omega_k(n)$".

lean.statement: Let $F$ be a complex-valued function on a finite-dimensional real inner product space $V$ and $\omega : \mathbb R \to V$. An *angle* of $F \circ \omega$ is a continuous $\theta : [0, 1] \to \mathbb R$ with $\theta(0) = 0$ and $F(\omega(t)) = e^{i\theta(t)}$ for $t \in [0, 1]$. An angle is unique, and it exists whenever $t \mapsto F(\omega(t))$ is continuous on $[0, 1]$, of modulus $1$, with $F(\omega(0)) = 1$. For $N \subseteq V$, points $p$, $q$ and a real $w$, let $\Omega_w \subseteq \Omega(N; p, q)$ be the set of paths $\omega$ for which $F \circ \omega$ has an angle with $\theta(1) = w$. If $F$ is continuous and $|F| = 1$ on a compact set containing $N$, every $\Omega_w$ is open and closed in $\Omega(N; p, q)$; and $\Omega_w$, $\Omega_{w'}$ are disjoint for $w \neq w'$.

diff: Theorem 22.1 is applied to one class of paths, which must be open and closed in the path space (V13.16). The classes are defined by the end value of the continuous angle of $F \circ \omega$, and are open and closed for every continuous $F$ of modulus $1$.

items.title: The complex determinant of a real matrix

milnor.label: §24, pp. 146–147
milnor.statement: Make $\mathbb R^n$ into an $(n/2)$-dimensional complex vector space by $iv = J_1J_2\cdots J_{k-1}v$. A unitary complex linear transformation "has a well defined complex determinant", and $f(J\exp(\pi tA)) = \det(\exp(\pi tA)) = e^{\pi t\operatorname{trace}A}$.

lean.statement: For real $n \times n$ matrices $\mathbf i$ and $M$ put $\det_{\mathbb C}M = \det(M_{\mathbb C}P_+ + P_-)$, a complex number, where $M_{\mathbb C}$ is $M$ read as a complex matrix and $P_\pm = \tfrac12(1 \mp \sqrt{-1}\,\mathbf i_{\mathbb C})$. Then $\det_{\mathbb C}I = 1$, and, if $\mathbf i^2 = -I$: $\det_{\mathbb C}(MN) = \det_{\mathbb C}M\,\det_{\mathbb C}N$ whenever $N$ commutes with $\mathbf i$; $|\det_{\mathbb C}M| = 1$ when $\mathbf i$ is skew and $M$ is orthogonal and commutes with $\mathbf i$; and $\det_{\mathbb C}\exp(tV) = e^{-\sqrt{-1}\,t\operatorname{tr}(V\mathbf i)/2}$ for every real $t$, when $V$ commutes with $\mathbf i$ and $\operatorname{tr}V = 0$.

diff: $\det_{\mathbb C}M = \det(M_{\mathbb C}P_+ + P_-)$, with $P_\pm$ the projections onto the $\pm\sqrt{-1}$-eigenspaces of $\mathbf i$ in $\mathbb C^n$. The complex trace of $V$ is $\tfrac12(\operatorname{tr}V - \sqrt{-1}\operatorname{tr}(V\mathbf i))$, so Milnor's $e^{\pi t\operatorname{trace}A}$ is $e^{-\sqrt{-1}\,\pi t\operatorname{tr}(A\mathbf i)/2}$.

items.title: Milnor's $i$ and $f$, and the classes $\Omega^{(c)}$

milnor.label: §24, pp. 146–148
milnor.statement: $iv = J_1J_2\cdots J_{k-1}v$; "the condition $k \equiv 2 \pmod 4$ guarantees that $i^2 = -1$, and that $J_1, J_2, \dots, J_{k-1}$ commute with $i$". For $J' \in \Omega_k(n)$ the composition $J^{-1}J'$ commutes with $i$, and $f(J') = \det_{\mathbb C}(J^{-1}J') \in S^1$. A component of $\Omega\Omega_k(n)$ is fixed by $\operatorname{trace}A = icm_k/2$.

lean.statement: Call a matrix $\mathbf i$ *central for $k$* if $\mathbf i^2 = -I$, $\mathbf i^{\mathsf T} = -\mathbf i$, $\mathbf i$ commutes with $J_1, \dots, J_{k-1}$ and with every matrix that commutes with all of them, and $\mathbf i$ anticommutes with every matrix that anticommutes with all of them. The product $\mathbf i = J_1J_2\cdots J_{k-1}$ is central for $k = 2$ when $J_1$ is a complex structure, and for $k = 6$ when $J_1, \dots, J_5$ is an anticommuting family. Let $\mathbf i$ be central for $k \ge 1$, $p \in \Omega_k(n)$, and $f(X) = \det_{\mathbb C}(p^{\mathsf T}X)$ (V15.34 with this $\mathbf i$). Then $|f| = 1$ on $\Omega_k(n)$, $f(p) = 1$, and $f(p\exp(tV)) = e^{-\sqrt{-1}\,t\operatorname{tr}(V\mathbf i)/2}$ for $V \in \mathcal T_p$. Now let $J_1, \dots, J_k$ be an anticommuting family, $k \ge 1$, $p = J_k$, $N$ the stratum through $J_k$, and let $\Omega_w \subseteq \Omega(N; J_k, -J_k)$ be the set of paths whose $f$-angle ends at $w$ (V15.33). Each $\Omega_w$ is open and closed, different $w$ give disjoint sets, and a path that agrees on $[0, 1]$ with $t \mapsto J_k\exp(tV)$, $V \in \mathcal T_{J_k}$, lies in $\Omega_w$ if and only if $w = -\operatorname{tr}(V\mathbf i)/2$. For an integer $c$, $\Omega^{(c)}$ denotes $\Omega_w$ with $w = \pi m_{k+1}c/2$.

diff: The properties of $i$ that are used (it commutes with everything commuting with $J_1, \dots, J_{k-1}$, and anticommutes with everything anticommuting with them) are proved for $k = 2$ and $k = 6$.

$\Omega^{(c)}$ is the set of paths whose $f$-angle ends at $\pi m_{k+1}c/2$. It is open and closed, and contains the geodesic $J_k\exp(\pi tA)$ exactly when $-\operatorname{tr}(A\mathbf i) = m_kc$, which is Milnor's $\operatorname{trace}A = icm_k/2$.

items.title: Every path lies in exactly one $\Omega^{(c)}$

milnor.label: §24, p. 148
milnor.statement: "Let us look only at matrices $A$ such that $\operatorname{trace}A = icm_k/2$ where $c$ is some constant integer."

lean.statement: Let $k = 2$ or $k = 6$, let $J_1, \dots, J_k$ be an anticommuting family, $\mathbf i = J_1\cdots J_{k-1}$ and $N$ the stratum through $J_k$. Every path in $\Omega(N; J_k, -J_k)$ lies in $\Omega^{(c)}$ for exactly one integer $c$. For $k = 6$ the proof uses that $f = G^4$ on $\Omega_6(n)$, where $G(X) = \det\bigl((J_6^{\mathsf T}X)_{\mathbb C}Q + 1 - Q\bigr)$ and $Q$ is the product of the projections $P_+$ of V15.34 for $\mathbf i$, $J_1J_2$ and $J_3J_4$.

chips: $c$ is an integer for every path
diff: For an arbitrary path the end angle is a multiple of $2\pi$ because $f(-J_k) = 1$ (as $4 \mid n$): Milnor's "closed loop". For $k = 6$ the normalization needs multiples of $4\pi$, which holds because $f$ is the fourth power of a continuous function on $\Omega_6(n)$.

items.title: The pieces for $k \equiv 2 \pmod 4$

milnor.label: §24, p. 147
milnor.statement: On each $M_h$ the complex linear transformation $A|M_h$ "can have only one eigenvalue, say $ia_h$", so $A|M_h$ coincides with $a_hJ_1J_2\cdots J_{k-1}|M_h$. $M_h$ is minimal under $J_1, \dots, J_{k-1}, J$, of complex dimension $m_k/2$; therefore $\operatorname{trace}A = i(a_1 + \dots + a_r)m_k/2$. In the setting of V15.29 (ii) with $k \ge 1$, let $\mathbf i = J_1\cdots J_{k-1}$ and suppose that $\mathbf i$ is skew-adjoint with $\mathbf i^2 = -1$, commutes with $A$ and the $J_\alpha$, and anticommutes with $J$. (i) On each minimal invariant $M$, $A = c\,\mathbf i$ for a real $c$. (ii) For matrices: if $\mathbf i$ is skew with $\mathbf i^2 = -I$ and commutes with $A$, $\exp(\pi A) = -I$, and $Aw = c\,\mathbf iw$ for a vector $w

milnor.statement: $2\lambda \ge \sum_{a_h > a_j}(a_h - a_j - 2)$. "Suppose for example that some $a_h$ is equal to $-3$": then $4\lambda \ge 2p \ge r + c$, where $r = n/m_k$ tends to infinity with $n$.

Let $J_1, \dots, J_k$ be an anticommuting family on $\mathbb R^n$ with $1 \le k \le 7$, $k

milnor.label: §24, p. 148
milnor.statement: "The component of $\Omega\Omega_k(n)$ is approximated up to higher and higher dimensions by the corresponding component of $\Omega_{k+1}(n)$, as $n \to \infty$."

Let $k = 2$ or $k = 6$, let $J_1, \dots, J_{k+1}$ be an anticommuting family on $\mathbb R^n$, $

items.title: Lemma 24.6 (8): $\Omega_8(16r) \cong O(r)$

milnor.statement: $\Omega_8(16r)$ can be identified with the set of all real isometries from $X_1$ to $X_2$: $J_7J_8$ maps $X_1$ isomorphically onto $X_2$, and "clearly this isomorphism determines $J_8$ uniquely". Thus $\Omega_8(16r)$ is diffeomorphic to the orthogonal group $O(r)$.

The commutant on $\mathbb R^{16}$ is found by a finite check on the $256$ Kronecker words.

items.title: Bott's chain at $n = 16r$

milnor.label: §24, Theorem 24.5, p. 138; p. 142
milnor.statement: $\pi_hO \cong \pi_{h-1}\Omega_1 \cong \pi_{h-2}\Omega_2 \cong \dots \cong \pi_1\Omega_{h-1}$; and $\Omega_8$ is homeomorphic to the infinite orthogonal group $O$, "combining this fact with Theorem 24.5".

items.title: Stability of $\pi_iO(n)$ and $\pi_iU(n)$

milnor.label: §23, proof of Lemma 23.4, pp. 128–129
milnor.statement: $\pi_{i-1}U(m) \cong \pi_{i-1}U(m + 1)$ for $i \le 2m$, from the fibration $U(m) \to U(m + 1) \to S^{2m+1}$. For $O$ no such statement is made: $\pi_iO$ is the homotopy group of the direct limit.

lean.statement: Let $\mathbb K = \mathbb R$ with $d = 1$, or $\mathbb K = \mathbb C$ with $d = 2$, and let $U_{\mathbb K}(m)$ be $O(m)$, resp. $U(m)$. If $i + 2 \le dm + d - 1$ and $i + 2 \le dm' + d - 1$, there is a bijection $\pi_i(U_{\mathbb K}(m), I) \cong \pi_i(U_{\mathbb K}(m'), I)$. milnor.statement: The infinite orthogonal group $O$ has the same homotopy type as its own 8-th loop space. Hence the homotopy group $\pi_iO$ is isomorphic to $\pi_{i+8}O$ for $i \ge 0$.

milnor.statement: $\pi_{i-1}U \cong \pi_{i+1}U$ for $i \ge 1$, where $\pi_{i-1}U = \pi_{i-1}U(m)$ for $i \le 2m$.

items.title: The telescope and homotopy direct limits

milnor.label: Appendix, p. 149
milnor.statement: For a topological space $X$ and a sequence $X_0 \subset X_1 \subset X_2 \subset \cdots$ of subspaces, it is convenient to consider the infinite union $X_\Sigma = X_0 \times [0, 1] \cup X_1 \times [1, 2] \cup X_2 \times [2, 3] \cup \cdots$, "to be topologized as a subset of $X \times \mathbb R$". Definition: $X$ is the *homotopy direct limit* of the sequence $\{X_i\}$ if the projection map $p : X_\Sigma \to X$, $p(x, \tau) = x$, is a homotopy equivalence.

lean.statement: Spaces are arbitrary topological spaces, with no separation axiom unless stated; for subsets $X_0, X_1, \dots$ of $X$, the telescope is $X_\Sigma = \bigcup_nX_n \times [n, n + 1] \subseteq X \times \mathbb R$, with the subspace topology; the $n$-th strip is the map $X_n \times [0, 1] \to X_\Sigma$, $(x, t) \mapsto (x, n + t)$; $p(x, \tau) = x$; and $X$ is the homotopy direct limit of $\{X_i\}$ if $p$ is a homotopy equivalence. **(T1)** For a monotone sequence, $(x, \tau) \in X_\Sigma$ iff $x \in X_n$ for some integer $0 \le n \le \tau$; so raising $\tau$ stays in $X_\Sigma$.

diff: The definition is Milnor's; the elementary fact (T1), that a point of the telescope may be raised, is used throughout his proof without comment and is stated here.

items.title: Pasting maps along the strips (T3)

milnor.label: Appendix, pp. 151–153
milnor.statement: The book has no such statement. Every map and homotopy on a telescope in the proof of Theorem A (pp. 151–153) is given strip by strip, by formulas in $(x, n + t)$, $0 \le t \le 1$, and its continuity is taken for granted.

lean.statement: Spaces are arbitrary topological spaces, with no separation axiom unless stated; if every $X_n$ is closed in $X$, then for every space $P$ a function $F$ on $P \times X_\Sigma$ is continuous as soon as each $(p, x, t) \mapsto F(p, (x, n + t))$ is continuous on $P \times X_n \times [0, 1]$. Hence, for a monotone sequence of closed sets, maps $\Phi_n : P \times X_n \times [0, 1] \to Z$ with $\Phi_{n+1}(p, x, 0) = \Phi_n(p, x, 1)$ define a continuous map on $P \times X_\Sigma$; in particular maps on $X_\Sigma$, and homotopies between them, may be given strip by strip.

diff: This is where closedness enters, a hypothesis Milnor never states: when the $X_n$ are closed, the strips are closed in $X_\Sigma$ and form a locally finite family, and pasting is legitimate. Without it Milnor's maps can be discontinuous (VA.10); the device that removes the hypothesis altogether is the mapping telescope (VA.13, VA.15).

items.title: The map of telescopes, and “clearly sufficient”

milnor.label: Appendix, proof of Theorem A, p. 150
milnor.statement: Define $f_\Sigma : X_\Sigma \to Y_\Sigma$ by $f_\Sigma(x, t) = (f(x), t)$. Then "it is clearly sufficient to prove that $f_\Sigma$ is a homotopy equivalence".

lean.statement: Spaces are arbitrary topological spaces, with no separation axiom unless stated; if $f : X \to Y$ carries each $X_n$ into $Y_n$, then $f_\Sigma(x, \tau) = (f(x), \tau)$ is a map $X_\Sigma \to Y_\Sigma$ with $p_Yf_\Sigma = fp_X$. If $X$ and $Y$ are the homotopy direct limits of $\{X_i\}$ and $\{Y_i\}$ and $f_\Sigma$ is a homotopy equivalence, then so is $f$.

diff: No hidden hypothesis: neither closedness nor monotonicity is needed. The proof is $f \simeq fp_Xs = p_Yf_\Sigma s$ for a homotopy inverse $s$ of $p_X$.

items.title: Truncations of the telescope (T2)

milnor.label: Appendix, p. 152
milnor.statement: In Case 2, $X_\Sigma^n$ is the subset of $X_\Sigma$ of pairs $(x, \tau)$ with $\tau \le n$, i.e. $X_0 \times [0, 1] \cup \dots \cup X_{n-1} \times [n - 1, n] \cup X_n \times [n]$. "In fact $X_\Sigma^n$ contains $X_n \times [n]$ as deformation retract", and the composition $Gf_\Sigma$ carries $X_\Sigma^n$ into itself.

lean.statement: Spaces are arbitrary topological spaces, with no separation axiom unless stated; the truncation $X^n_\Sigma = \{(x, \tau) \in X_\Sigma : \tau \le n\}$ is closed in $X_\Sigma$, and $X^0_\Sigma \subseteq X^1_\Sigma \subseteq \cdots$, whatever the $X_i$. For a monotone sequence, $x \mapsto (x, n)$ is a homotopy equivalence $X_n \to X^n_\Sigma$ with homotopy inverse $(x, \tau) \mapsto x$, the homotopy raising $\tau$ to $n$; and a function on $X_\Sigma$ that sends the $n$-th strip to levels $\le n + 1$ and $X_n \times \{n\}$ to levels $\le n$ sends each $X^m_\Sigma$ to levels $\le m$.

diff: The two facts Milnor states are proved; the deformation retraction is stated as a homotopy equivalence, its homotopy being the one that raises $\tau$ to $n$.
That truncations are always closed, with no closedness of the $X_i$, is what lets Case 2 need closedness only of the $Y_i$ (VA.11).

items.title: A level function makes a homotopy direct limit (Lemmas 2.1, 2.2)

milnor.label: Appendix, Example 1, p. 149
milnor.statement: In Example 1, given $f : X \to \mathbb R$ with $f(x) \ge i + 1$ for $x \notin X_i$ and $f \ge 0$, the correspondence $x \mapsto (x, f(x))$ maps $X$ homeomorphically onto a subset of $X_\Sigma$ "which is clearly a deformation retract". At the end of Case 2 (p. 153), Case 1 is applied to the sequence of truncations $\{X_\Sigma^n\}$, which uses that $X_\Sigma$ is their homotopy direct limit.

lean.statement: Spaces are arbitrary topological spaces, with no separation axiom unless stated; (i) for a monotone sequence, if $f : X \to \mathbb R$ is continuous, $f \ge 0$, and $f(x) \ge n + 1$ whenever $x \notin X_n$, then $X$ is the homotopy direct limit of $\{X_i\}$. (ii) For any sequence, $X_\Sigma$ is the homotopy direct limit of its truncations $\{X^n_\Sigma\}$.

items.title: Example 1, and sublevel sets

milnor.label: Appendix, Example 1
milnor.statement: Suppose that each point of $X$ lies in the interior of some $X_i$, and that $X$ is paracompact. Then using a partition of unity one can construct a map $f : X \to \mathbb R$ so that $f(x) \ge i + 1$ for $x \notin X_i$ and $f(x) \ge 0$ for all $x$; and $X$ is a homotopy direct limit.

lean.statement: Spaces are arbitrary topological spaces, with no separation axiom unless stated; (i) let $X$ be paracompact and Hausdorff, and $X_0 \subseteq X_1 \subseteq \cdots$ with every point of $X$ in the interior of some $X_i$; then $X$ is the homotopy direct limit of $\{X_i\}$. (ii) Let $E : X \to \mathbb R$ be continuous, on any space $X$, and $a_0 \le a_1 \le \cdots$ with $a_i \to \infty$. Then $X$ is the homotopy direct limit of the sublevel sets $\{x : E(x) \le a_i\}$.

In (i) Milnor's "paracompact" is read with the Hausdorff axiom, as Mathlib's partitions of unity need a normal space.

items.title: Example 3

milnor.label: Appendix, Example 3
milnor.statement: The unit interval $[0, 1]$ is not the homotopy direct limit of the sequence of closed subsets $[0] \cup [1/i, 1]$. No proof is given.

lean.statement: Let $X_n = \{0\} \cup [\frac1{n+1}, 1] \subseteq [0, 1]$. The $X_n$ are closed and increasing, with union $[0, 1]$, and $[0, 1]$ is not the homotopy direct limit of $\{X_n\}$.

items.title: Milnor’s maps $h_1$ and their homotopy inverse $g$

milnor.label: Appendix, Case 1, pp. 151–152
milnor.statement: Any map $h_1 : X_\Sigma \to X_\Sigma$ with $h_1(x, n + t) = (x, n + 2t)$ for $0 \le t \le \frac12$ and $h_1(x, n + t) \in X_{n+1} \times [n + 1]$ for $\frac12 \le t \le 1$ is a homotopy equivalence, with homotopy inverse $g(x, n + t) = (x, n + 2t)$ for $t \le \frac12$, $h_1(x, n + \frac32 - t)$ for $t \ge \frac12$, well defined since $h_1(x, n + \frac12) = h_1(x, n + 1) = (x, n + 1)$. $h_1g \simeq \mathrm{id}$ by a homotopy $H_u$, $0 \le u \le \frac12$, ending at $(x, n + \min(4t, 1))$, "clearly" homotopic to the identity; $gh_1 \simeq \mathrm{id}$ "by a completely analogous argument".

lean.statement: Spaces are arbitrary topological spaces, with no separation axiom unless stated; let $X_0 \subseteq X_1 \subseteq \cdots$ be closed in $X$. (i) For a map $\rho : I \to I$ with $\rho(0) = 0$, $\rho(1) = 1$, $(x, n + t) \mapsto (x, n + \rho(t))$ is homotopic to the identity of $X_\Sigma$. (ii) Let $\psi : X_\Sigma \to X_\Sigma$ be a map with $\psi(x, n + t) = (x, n + 2t)$ for $t \le \frac12$ and $\psi(x, n + t)$ at level $n + 1$ for $t \ge \frac12$. Then $\psi$ fixes the points at integer levels and is a homotopy equivalence, with homotopy inverse Milnor's $g$.

items.title: Theorem A, Case 1, and a possible misprint $(4 - 3t)u$

milnor.label: Appendix, Case 1, pp. 150–152
milnor.statement: Case 1: suppose that $X_i = Y_i$ and that each $f_i : X_i \to Y_i$ is homotopic to the identity; then $f_\Sigma$ is a homotopy equivalence. With one-parameter families $h^n_u : X_n \to X_n$, $h^n_0 = f_n$, $h^n_1 = \mathrm{id}$, the homotopy $h_u : X_\Sigma \to X_\Sigma$ is $(h^n_u(x), n + 2t)$ for $0 \le t \le \frac12$, $(h^n_{(3-4t)u}(x), n + 1)$ for $\frac12 \le t \le \frac34$, and $(h^{n+1}_{(4-3t)u}(x), n + 1)$ for $\frac34 \le t \le 1$. "Taking $u = 0$ this defines a map $h_0$ which is clearly homotopic to $f_\Sigma$", and $h_1$ has the properties of VA.9.

With homotopies $h^n_u$ from $\varphi_n$ to the identity, the homotopy is $(h^n_u(x), n + 2t)$ for $t \le \frac12$, $(h^n_{(3-4t)u}(x), n + 1)$ for $\frac12 \le t \le \frac34$, and $(h^{n+1}_{(4t-3)u}(x), n + 1)$ for $\frac34 \le t \le 1$; it is continuous in $(u, z)$, $h_0 = \varphi_\Sigma \circ R_2$ is homotopic to $\varphi_\Sigma$, and $h_1$ is a map as in VA.9.

items.title: Theorem A, Case 2: $f_\Sigma$ is a homotopy equivalence

milnor.label: Appendix, Case 2, pp. 152–153
milnor.statement: Now let $X$ and $Y$ be arbitrary. With homotopy inverses $g_n$ of the $f_n$, $i_ng_n \simeq g_{n+1}f_{n+1}i_ng_n = g_{n+1}j_nf_ng_n \simeq g_{n+1}j_n$; with a homotopy $h^n_u$ from $i_ng_n$ to $g_{n+1}j_n$, $G(y, n + t) = (g_n(y), n + 2t)$ for $t \le \frac12$ and $(h^n_{2t-1}(y), n + 1)$ for $t \ge \frac12$. $Gf_\Sigma$ carries $X^n_\Sigma$ into itself by a map homotopic to the identity, so "we can apply Case 1 to the sequence $\{X_\Sigma^n\}$, and conclude that $Gf_\Sigma$ is a homotopy equivalence"; similarly $f_\Sigma G$; so $f_\Sigma$ has a left and a right homotopy inverse.

(ii) Let $X_0 \subseteq X_1 \subseteq \cdots$ in $X$ and $Y_0 \subseteq Y_1 \subseteq \cdots$ in $Y$, the $Y_n$ closed, and let $f : X \to Y$ carry each $X_n$ into $Y_n$ by a homotopy equivalence $f_n$. items.title: Theorem A, by Milnor’s proof

milnor.statement: Suppose that $X$ is the homotopy direct limit of $\{X_i\}$ and $Y$ is the homotopy direct limit of $\{Y_i\}$. Let $f : X \to Y$ be a map which carries each $X_i$ into $Y_i$ by a homotopy equivalence. Then $f$ itself is a homotopy equivalence.
